paras.en: [[9:15|And Jesus said to them: Can the children of the bridegroom|Et ait illis Jesus: Numquid possunt filii sponsi]], that is, My spiritual sons and disciples, I who am the Bridegroom of the Church (of whom we read: [[Ps 18:6|as a bridegroom coming out of his bridechamber|Tanquam sponsus procedens de thalamo suo]]; of whom the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 11:2|I have espoused you to one husband that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ|Despondi vos uni viro virginem castam exhibere Christo]]), [[9:15|mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them|lugere quamdiu cum illis est sponsus]], that is, be afflicted and saddened by fasting often and keeping up other rigorous exercises? As if to say: This is not fitting; [[John 3:29|but the friend of the bridegroom, who standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth with joy because of the bridegroom's voice|amicus autem et filius sponsi, qui stat et audit eum, gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi]]. [[9:15|But the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them|Veniet autem tempus quum auferetur ab eis sponsus]], that is, the day of the passion and ascension, when Christ was taken away as to His bodily presence, as He says: [[Matt 26:11|For the poor you have always with you: but me you have not always|Pauperes semper habebitis vobiscum, me autem non semper habebitis]]; and again: [[John 16:28|I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world: again I leave the world, and I go to the Father|Exivi a Patre, et veni in mundum; iterum relinquo mundum, et vado ad Patrem]]. But as to the nature of the divine majesty, and His gracious and spiritual indwelling, He always was and is with His faithful, according to that saying: [[Matt 28:20|behold I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world|ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem sæculi]]. [[9:15|and then they shall fast|Et tunc jejunabunt]], abstaining bodily: as did James, who vowed that he would not eat until he had seen the Son of man risen from the dead [this story is told by St Jerome, De viris illustribus 2, from the Gospel according to the Hebrews], and Peter, who [[Matt 26:75|going forth, he wept bitterly|egressus flevit amare]], until he heard that Christ had risen. And it is certain that the Apostles, and the whole primitive Church, lived in great sobriety after Christ's passion.

paras.t: Insuper probat Christus, per quasdam similitudines, quod discipulis suis adhuc non congruebat frequens vel magnum jejunium. Nemo autem prudenter agens, immittit, id est, suendo transfert et inserit, commissuram, id est juncturam seu particulam, panni rudis, id est novi, pilosi, ac spissi, in vestimentum vetus, illud reformando cum tali particula a novo panno seu vestimento abrupta. Tollit enim plenitudinem ejus a vestimento, id est, si quis partem panni novi a nova veste acceptam, adjungat et consuat veteri vestimento, aufert plenitudinem ejus, id est perfectionem novi panni, a vestimento novo, quod deformatur et partim corrumpitur, si ei pars sua abstrahatur, ut veteri vesti jungatur; et pejor scissura, id est damnosior corruptio, fit in novo panno seu vestimento, quam fuerat in antiquo. Per hoc innuit Christus, quod sicut tam differentium pannorum conjunctio improportionata est et deformis, sic status jejunantium non potest subito transferri in eos qui usitati sunt manducare frequenter, quales fuerunt discipuli Christi. Idcirco oportuit eos primo spiritualiter innovari per Spiritum Sanctum, tuncque abstinere: sicut et factum est. Nam statim post resurrectionem, receperunt Spiritum Sanctum insufflante in eos Christo: quem in die Pentecostes plenius receperunt; et ex tunc jejunaverunt. Istud videmus quotidie verificari, quod homines quamvis pœniteant multum, tamen jejunare non valent, nisi per gratiam confortentur ac renoventur.
paras.en: Further, Christ proves by certain comparisons that frequent or great fasting did not yet suit His disciples. [[9:16|And nobody putteth|Nemo autem prudenter agens, immittit]], no one acting prudently, that is, transfers and inserts by sewing, [[9:16|a piece|commissuram]], that is, a joining-piece or small part, [[9:16|of raw cloth|panni rudis]], that is, new, shaggy and thick, [[9:16|unto an old garment|in vestimentum vetus]], mending it with such a piece torn from new cloth or a new garment. [[9:16|For it taketh away the fulness thereof from the garment|Tollit enim plenitudinem ejus a vestimento]]: that is, if anyone takes a part of new cloth from a new garment and joins and sews it to an old garment, he takes away its fulness, that is, the completeness of the new cloth, from the new garment, which is disfigured and partly spoiled if a part of it is drawn off to be joined to the old garment; [[9:16|and there is made a greater rent|et pejor scissura fit]], that is, a more harmful damage, in the new cloth or garment than there was in the old. By this Christ hints that, just as the joining of such different cloths is ill-matched and unsightly, so the state of those who fast cannot be suddenly transferred to those who are used to eating often, as Christ's disciples were. Therefore they had first to be spiritually renewed by the Holy Ghost, and then to abstain; and so it was done. For immediately after the resurrection they received the Holy Ghost, Christ breathing on them[[John 20:22||]] [the margin prints Joann. xx, 23; the breathing is in v. 22], whom they received more fully on the day of Pentecost[[Acts 2:1||]]; and from then on they fasted. We see this verified every day: men, however much they repent, cannot fast unless they are strengthened and renewed by grace.

paras.t: Aliud exemplum subjungitur. Neque mittunt, id est, homines non fundunt, vinum novum, videlicet mustum, in utres veteres, id est in vasa antiqua. Alioquin, id est, si mustum in veteres utres transfundatur, rumpuntur utres tales, quum sint debiles, vini violentam ebullitionem non potentes sufferre, et vinum effunditur, et utres tales pereunt, id est, destruuntur. Sed vinum novum in utres novos mittunt homines, et ambo conservantur, id est, vinum et vasa manent in esse. Per hoc Salvator insinuat, quod sicut debilia vasa ferre nequeunt nova vina, sic rudes et fragiles discipuli sui nondum dispositi erant ad sustinendum magnum rigorem jejunii; sed innovandi erant per infusionem Spiritus Sancti, quatenus fervorem perfectionis, abstinentiæque rigorem, utiliter et fructuose possent sufferre: quia Joannis et Pharisæorum discipuli, quamvis corporaliter jejunabant, parum tamen interius profecerunt, quoniam gratia innovationis prædictæ non erant repleti. Tali ergo infructuoso jejunio noluit Christus suos vexari, præsertim quum corporalis exercitatio ad modica prosit. Per vinum igitur novum, rigor abstinentiæ et fervor perfectionis designantur; per utres veteres, homines fragiles, nondum spiritualiter renovati, roborati, accensi. Idcirco ferre non possunt rigorem justitiæ et perfectionis laborem, sed rumpuntur, quia sub onere cadunt, nisi mirabiliter præveniantur a Spiritu Sancto. Propterea paulatim ad perfectionem ducendi sunt: sicut novitiis in religione conceditur annus probationis, in quo vires proprias experiantur, et pedetentim ad perfectiora exercitia extendantur. Nam et paulatim longius itur. Et Bernardus ait: Nolo subito summus fieri; successive proficere volo.
paras.en: Another example is added. [[9:17|Neither do they put|Neque mittunt]], that is, men do not pour, [[9:17|new wine|vinum novum]], that is, must, [[9:17|into old bottles|in utres veteres]], that is, into old vessels. [[9:17|Otherwise|Alioquin]], that is, if must is poured into old wineskins, [[9:17|the bottles break|rumpuntur utres]], such skins, being weak and unable to bear the violent fermenting of the wine, [[9:17|and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish|et vinum effunditur, et utres tales pereunt]], that is, are destroyed. [[9:17|But new wine they put into new bottles|Sed vinum novum in utres novos mittunt]], men do, [[9:17|and both are preserved|et ambo conservantur]], that is, both wine and vessels remain in being. By this the Saviour suggests that, as weak vessels cannot bear new wine, so His untaught and frail disciples were not yet disposed to bear the great rigour of fasting, but had to be renewed by the infusion of the Holy Ghost, so that they might bear the fervour of perfection and the rigour of abstinence usefully and fruitfully: for the disciples of John and of the Pharisees, though they fasted bodily, made little progress inwardly, because they were not filled with the grace of the said renewal. With such fruitless fasting, then, Christ would not have His own wearied, especially since [[1 Tim 4:8|bodily exercise is profitable to little|corporalis exercitatio ad modica prosit]]. So by the new wine are signified the rigour of abstinence and the fervour of perfection; by the old bottles, frail men, not yet spiritually renewed, strengthened and set on fire. Therefore they cannot bear the rigour of justice and the labour of perfection, but burst, because they fall under the burden, unless they are wonderfully prevented [that is, gone before and helped] by the Holy Ghost. They must therefore be led to perfection little by little, as novices in religion are granted a year of probation, in which to try their own strength and to be drawn on step by step to more perfect exercises. For one goes further by degrees. And Bernard says: I do not wish to become the highest all at once; I wish to advance step by step.

paras.t: Hæc verba jam præinducta, illo, videlicet Christo, loquente ad illos discipulos Joannis Baptistæ, ecce princeps unus accessit ad Jesum corde fideli, et corpore celeri. Secundum Lucam et Marcum, princeps iste fuit archisynagogus seu princeps synagogæ cujusdam, vocabaturque Jairus. Habebant enim Judei certas domos seu templa, non ad sacrificia offerenda, sed ad vacandum orationi, lectioni, consilio ac laudibus Dei: et hæ domus vocata sunt synagogæ. Qui vero præerant synagogis et eis qui ad synagogas confluxerunt, nominabantur archisynagogi: quorum unus exstitit Jairus iste. Et adoravit eum, videlicet Christum: non adoratione latriæ, quia non putavit Jesum esse Deum. Nam ut ex subditis innotescit, non putavit eum posse facere quod rogabatur, nisi corporaliter esset præsens. Adoravit igitur eum, id est, magnam ei reverentiam exhibebat: cecidit enim ad pedes ejus, ut Lucas refert. Juxta quod scriptum est: Quanto major es, humilia te in omnibus. Sed quæritur, si non credidit Jesum esse Deum, quomodo mente fideli accessit. Et respondendum, quod credidit eum posse facere quod rogabatur: nec Jairus tenebatur adhuc ad tam explicitam fidem, ut ideo dicatur non fuisse fidelis, quia non credidit Jesum esse Deum.
paras.en: [[9:18|As he was speaking these things unto them|Hæc … illo … loquente ad illos]], that is, as Christ was saying the words already given to those disciples of John the Baptist, [[9:18|behold a certain ruler came up|ecce princeps unus accessit]] to Jesus with a faithful heart and with swift body. According to Luke and Mark this ruler was an archisynagogue, that is, the ruler of a certain synagogue, and was called Jairus[[Luke 8:41||]][[Mark 5:22||]]. For the Jews had certain houses or temples, not for offering sacrifices, but for giving time to prayer, reading, counsel and the praises of God; and these houses were called synagogues. Those who were over the synagogues and over those who gathered at them were called archisynagogues, one of whom was this Jairus. [[9:18|and adored him|Et adoravit eum]], that is, Christ: not with the adoration of latria [the worship due to God alone], for he did not think Jesus to be God. For, as appears from what follows, he did not think Him able to do what was asked unless He were bodily present. He adored Him, then, that is, showed Him great reverence: for [[Luke 8:41|he fell down at the feet of Jesus|cecidit enim ad pedes ejus]], as Luke relates; according to what is written: [[Ecclus 3:20|The greater thou art, the more humble thyself in all things|Quanto major es, humilia te in omnibus]]. But it is asked, if he did not believe Jesus to be God, how he came with a faithful mind. It must be answered that he believed He could do what was asked; nor was Jairus as yet bound to so explicit a faith that he should be said not to have been faithful because he did not believe Jesus to be God.

paras.t: Accessit ergo, dicens: Domine, filia mea modo defuncta est. Videtur huic contrarium, quod in Marco legitur Christo dixisse: Filia mea in extremis est. Dicendum dupliciter: Primo, quod Jairus loquitur secundum communem modum loquendi, quo de agonizante cujus vita desperatur, communiter dicimus, quod sit mortuus homo. Jairo autem recedente a domo, cœpit filia ejus se ad mortem disponere: unde apud Lucam habetur, quod moriebatur. Idcirco asseruit eam defunctam. Secundo, quod Matthæus narrat verba Jairi qua dixit Christo, postquam a servis suis percepit filiam suam jam esse mortuam. Sed veni corporaliter, impone manum tuam super eam, et vivet, id est, resuscitabitur. Non ergo Jairus tam perfectæ fidei fuit sicut centurio, sed corporalem præsentiam Christi necessariam estimavit. Tantam vero virtutem ac sansanctitatem credidit inesse animæ Christi, ut corporali tactu suæ manus, filia ejus suscitaretur, utique virtute, prece ac merito anima Christi. Non enim ignoravit hic Jairus, quemadmodum in libris Regum legitur defunctum quemdam suscitatum ex contactu ossium Elisei.
paras.en: He came, then, [[9:18|saying: Lord, my daughter is even now dead|dicens: Domine, filia mea modo defuncta est]]. What we read in Mark seems contrary to this, that he said to Christ: [[Mark 5:23|My daughter is at the point of death|Filia mea in extremis est]]. It must be answered in two ways. First, that Jairus speaks according to the common way of speaking, by which we commonly say of someone in his agony, whose life is despaired of, that the man is dead. And when Jairus left his house, his daughter had begun to settle towards death: whence in Luke we have that [[Luke 8:42|she was dying|moriebatur]]. Therefore he asserted that she was dead. Secondly, that Matthew relates the words Jairus said to Christ after he had learned from his servants that his daughter was now dead. [[9:18|but come|Sed veni]] bodily, [[9:18|lay thy hand upon her, and she shall live|impone manum tuam super eam, et vivet]], that is, she will be raised again. So Jairus was not of such perfect faith as the centurion, but thought Christ's bodily presence necessary. Yet he believed such power and holiness to be in Christ's soul that by the bodily touch of His hand his daughter would be raised, by the power, prayer and merit of Christ's soul. For this Jairus was not ignorant that, as we read in the books of Kings, a certain dead man was raised by touching the bones of Eliseus[[4 Kings 13:21||]].

paras.t: Et surgens Jesus a domo Matthæi, in qua cum publicanis comedit, suosque, ut dictum est, discipulos excusavit, sequebatur eum, videlicet Jairum. Compatiebatur etenim Jairo, quia secundum Lucam, filia ista unica erat parentibus suis, habens annos fere duodecim. Videtur itaque Jairus præcessisse, quia nunc dicitur, quod Christus sequebatur eum. Tamen in Marco scriptum est, quod abiit cum eo; nec in hoc est dissonantia. Quamvis enim itinerantium unus ante alium vadat, nihilo minus simul ire dicuntur: et forte Jairus parum præcessit, quasi dispositurus domum suam ad recipiendum Christum condigne. Et discipuli ejus, videlicet Christi, simul cum suo magistro secuti sunt Jairum, imo et turba magna, secundum Marcum.
paras.en: [[9:19|And Jesus rising up|Et surgens Jesus]] from the house of Matthew, in which He ate with the publicans and, as has been said, excused His disciples, [[9:19|followed him|sequebatur eum]], that is, Jairus. For He had compassion on Jairus, because, according to Luke, this daughter was the only one her parents had, about twelve years old[[Luke 8:42||]]. So Jairus seems to have gone ahead, since it is now said that Christ followed him. Yet in Mark it is written that [[Mark 5:24|he went with him|abiit cum eo]]; nor is there any disagreement in this. For although, of people walking, one goes before another, they are none the less said to go together; and perhaps Jairus went a little ahead, as if to make his house ready to receive Christ worthily. [[9:19|with his disciples|Et discipuli ejus]], that is, Christ's, followed Jairus together with their Master, and indeed a great crowd too, according to Mark[[Mark 5:24||]].

paras.t: Et ecce mulier. Quum in divinis Scripturis premittitur, Ecce, innuitur notabile esse quod sequitur. Quæ sanguinis fluxum patiebatur, forte in naribus, duodecim annis. Et quum vita animalis consistat in sanguine, patet quod talis infirmitas sit periculosa atque letalis. Accessit retro: quia pre verecundia voluit occulte facere quod fecit, præsertim quum secundum legem, esset immunda; et tetigit fimbriam vestimenti ejus, hoc est inferiorem partem vestimenti. Hoc loco asserunt expositores, estque probabile, quod Christus portaverit vestimentum juxta consuetudinem Judæorum, videlicet cum quatuor fimbriis. Legitur quippe in Numeris, quod quum Dominus præcepisset hominem sabbato ligna colligentem lapidari, eo quod præceptum de sabbati celebratione fuisset transgressus, jussit Dominus ut filii Israel facerent sibi fimbrias quatuor, per quatuor angulos palliorum, ponentes in eis vittas hyacinthinas, quas quum viderent, recordarentur omnium præceptorum Domini. Hoc ad præcepta cæremonialia pertinebat: idcirco Christus factus sub lege, id observavit, sicut et alia quædam legalia, usque ad tempus passionis, in quo cæremonialium obligatio prorsus cessavit.
paras.en: [[9:20|And behold a woman|Et ecce mulier]]. When 'behold' is put first in the divine Scriptures, it suggests that what follows is noteworthy. [[9:20|who was troubled with an issue of blood twelve years|quæ sanguinis fluxum patiebatur duodecim annis]], perhaps from the nostrils. And since the life of an animal consists in the blood, it is plain that such an infirmity is dangerous and deadly. [[9:20|came behind him|Accessit retro]], because out of shame she wished to do secretly what she did, especially since according to the law she was unclean[[Lev 15:25||]]; [[9:20|and touched the hem of his garment|et tetigit fimbriam vestimenti ejus]], that is, the lower part of His garment. At this place the expositors assert, and it is probable, that Christ wore a garment according to the custom of the Jews, namely with four hems or tassels. For we read in Numbers that when the Lord had commanded that a man gathering sticks on the sabbath be stoned[[Num 15:32||]], because he had transgressed the precept of keeping the sabbath, the Lord ordered the children of Israel to make themselves four fringes at the four corners of their cloaks, putting in them ribbons of violet, so that when they saw them they might remember all the commandments of the Lord[[Num 15:38||]]. This belonged to the ceremonial precepts; therefore Christ, being [[Gal 4:4|made under the law|factus sub lege]], kept it, as He did certain other legal observances, up to the time of His passion, in which the obligation of the ceremonial precepts ceased altogether.

paras.t: Hanc mulierem dicit Ambrosius Martham fuisse. Sed videtur obsistere, quod apud Lucam mulier hæc fertur omnem substantiam suam in medicos erogasse. Martha vero post hujus miraculi perpetrationem dives fuit: aliter Christum et ejus comitivam tam frequenter ac liberaliter aluisse ac hospitasse non valuisset. Eusebius ergo in Ecclesiastica historia ait, quod fuit mulier civis Cæsareæ Philippi. In cujus testimonium dicit ante fores domus ejus erectam imaginem æream genibus provolutam, juxta quam est imago Salvatoris dexteram protendentis ad statuam […]
paras.en: Ambrose says this woman was Martha. But it seems to stand in the way that in Luke this woman is said to have [[Luke 8:43|bestowed all her substance on physicians|omnem substantiam suam in medicos erogasse]]. But Martha was rich after this miracle was done; otherwise she could not have fed and lodged Christ and His company so often and so liberally. So Eusebius says in his Ecclesiastical History that she was a woman, a citizen of Caesarea Philippi; in witness of which he says that before the doors of her house there was set up a bronze image of a woman on bended knees, and beside it an image of the Saviour stretching out His right hand towards the statue […] [some lines here are unreadable in the scan].

paras.t: Dicebat enim intra se, id est in corde: Si tetigero tantum vestimentum ejus, salva ero ab isto sanguinis diuturno profluvio. In quo magnitudo devotionis ac fidei hujus feminæ declaratur, quæ non solum per tactum manus, ut archisynagogus, sed etiam per tactum vestis Christi credidit omnem infirmitatem, quamvis naturaliter incurabilem, posse curari. Nam et iste sanguinis fluxus, naturaliter incurabilis fuit, ut patet ex ejus diuturnitate, et impotentia medicorum, in quos dum mulier omnia bona sua expendisset, nihil profecit, secundum Lucam. Tantam igitur credidit Christo sanctitatem ac potestatem inesse, […] se virtutem sanandi non haberet, tamen, in quantum erat operimentum corporis Christi, virtuosum et efficax fuit instrumentum curandi, interiori virtute redundante ad exteriora.
paras.en: [[9:21|For she said within herself|Dicebat enim intra se]], that is, in her heart: [[9:21|If I shall touch only his garment, I shall be healed|Si tetigero tantum vestimentum ejus, salva ero]] of this long-lasting issue of blood. In this is shown the greatness of this woman's devotion and faith, for she believed that every infirmity, even one naturally incurable, could be cured not only by the touch of His hand, as the archisynagogue believed, but even by the touch of Christ's garment. For this issue of blood was naturally incurable, as is clear from how long it had lasted and from the helplessness of the physicians, on whom the woman spent all her goods and gained nothing, according to Luke[[Luke 8:43||]]. Such holiness and power, then, she believed to be in Christ […] that, though the garment had of itself no power to heal, yet inasmuch as it was the covering of Christ's body, it was a powerful and effective instrument of healing, the inward power overflowing to the outward things.

paras.t: At Jesus conversus, id est, retro seu post se adspiciens, et videns eam oculo corporali, et notitia approbationis, dixit: Confide, filia, magis quam ante, id est, firmiter spera te obtinere quod cupis, atque majora. Invitat ergo eam potius ad robur augmentumque spei, quam ad ipsam spem: nam et ante confidebat; aliter non tetigisset. Lucas et Marcus plenius recitant istud miraculum, quia secundum eos, Christus interrogavit, Quis me tetigit? Et Petro respondente, Præceptor, turbæ te comprimunt et affligunt, et tu dicis, Quis me tetigit? Christus repetivit: Tetigit me aliquis; nam et ego novi virtutem de me exisse. Quo dicto, videns mulier quia non latuit, venit, procidit, et coram omnibus profitebatur quid fecit, et quomodo ei acciderit. Fides tua, id est actio fidei, te salvam fecit ab isto languore per modum causæ instrumentalis ac meritoriæ, id est, merito fidei tuæ curata es a me, tanquam a causa principali et efficienti. Et salva facta est mulier a profluvio sanguinis, et a peccatis, ex illa hora qua tetigit fimbriam ejus. Christus equidem, cujus per[…] salvavit in corpore, quamvis quidam eorum recidivum inciderint, redeundo ad vitia.
paras.en: [[9:22|But Jesus turning|At Jesus conversus]], that is, looking back or behind Him, [[9:22|and seeing her|et videns eam]] with His bodily eye and with the knowledge of approval, [[9:22|said: Be of good heart, daughter|dixit: Confide, filia]], more than before, that is, hope firmly that you will obtain what you desire, and greater things too. So He invites her rather to strength and increase of hope than to hope itself, for she had trusted before too; otherwise she would not have touched Him. Luke and Mark relate this miracle more fully, for according to them Christ asked, Who touched me? And when Peter answered, [[Luke 8:45|Master, the multitudes throng and press thee, and dost thou say, Who touched me?|Præceptor, turbæ te comprimunt et affligunt, et tu dicis, Quis me tetigit?]] Christ repeated: [[Luke 8:46|Somebody hath touched me; for I know that virtue is gone out from me|Tetigit me aliquis; nam et ego novi virtutem de me exisse]]. When He had said this, [[Luke 8:47|the woman seeing that she was not hid|videns mulier quia non latuit]], came, fell down, and confessed before all what she had done and how it had happened to her[[Mark 5:33||]]. [[9:22|thy faith|Fides tua]], that is, the act of faith, [[9:22|hath made thee whole|te salvam fecit]] of this sickness, by way of an instrumental and meritorious cause: that is, by the merit of your faith you have been cured by Me, as by the principal and efficient cause. [[9:22|And the woman was made whole|Et salva facta est mulier]] from the flow of blood and from her sins, [[9:22|from that hour|ex illa hora]] in which she touched the hem of His garment. Christ indeed, whose […] [two lines are unreadable in the scan here; the margin gives Deut. xxx, 4] healed in body, though some of them fell back again, returning to their vices.

paras.t: Moraliter per mulierem sanguine profluentem, intelligitur quælibet anima peccatrix, fluxu peccati atque immunditia contabescens: quæ a nullo viatore curari potest, sed tangendo fimbriam vestimenti Christi, id est sacramenta Salvatoris recipiendo, curatur.
paras.en: Morally, by the woman with the issue of blood is understood any sinful soul, wasting away with the flow and uncleanness of sin, which can be cured by no wayfarer [that is, by no one still in this life], but is cured by touching the hem of Christ's garment, that is, by receiving the Saviour's sacraments.

paras.t: Et quum venisset Jesus in domum principis, scilicet Jairi archisynagogi. Omittit Matthæus quod alii Evangelistæ pronuntiant, videlicet, quod Jesu exsistente in via, quidam venerunt, dicentes ad Jairum: […] vexas Magistrum? Putabant enim Jesum non posse suscitare defunctam, quamvis potuerit agonizantem sanare. Propter quod Jesus dixit ad Jairum: Noli timere. Tantummodo crede, et salva erit. Et quum vidisset tibicines, hoc est quosdam homines lugubre carmen canentes, ad provocandum fletum in aliis. Tales adducebantur antiquitus in funere magnarum personarum. Quemadmodum enim quædam symphoniæ, melodiæ, seu cantus provocant ad audaciam, sicut in bellis, quædam ad lætitiam, quædam ad devotionem; sic quædam inducunt ad planctum. et turbam tumultuantem, hoc est, confusum sonum, et magnum strepitum facientem, loquendo, lamentando, et funeri necessaria præparando; dicebat ad eos: Recedite, domum exeundo, et ab ista afflictione et tumultu cessando; non est enim puella mortua quoad me, quamvis naturali ordine mortua sit, sed dormit mihi, qui eam valeo facilius suscitare a morte, quam vos dormientem a somno. Itaque, Non est mortua, id est irreparabiliter destituta a vita, sed dormit, dormitione mortis, simili dormitioni somni. Et deridebant eum, scientes quod mortua esset. Laborabant enim in æquivocis, et non intellexerunt profunditatem verborum Christi. Et forte puella ista non fuit mortua morte culpæ, quamvis fuerit mortua morte naturæ, ut ideo quoque dictum sit: Non est mortua, sed dormit.
paras.en: [[9:23|And when Jesus was come into the house of the ruler|Et quum venisset Jesus in domum principis]], namely of Jairus the archisynagogue. Matthew leaves out what the other Evangelists declare, namely that while Jesus was on the way, certain men came and said to Jairus[[Luke 8:49||]]: […] [a line is unreadable in the scan here; in Mark the words run: Thy daughter is dead: why dost thou trouble the master any further?] … [[Mark 5:35|trouble the master|vexas Magistrum]]? For they thought Jesus could not raise a dead girl, though He could have healed one in her agony. Wherefore Jesus said to Jairus: [[Mark 5:36|Fear not, only believe|Noli timere. Tantummodo crede]], [[Luke 8:50|and she shall be safe|et salva erit]]. [[9:23|and saw the minstrels|Et quum vidisset tibicines]], that is, certain men singing a mournful song to move others to weeping. Such men were brought in of old at the funerals of great persons. For just as certain harmonies, melodies or songs rouse men to boldness, as in wars, others to gladness, others to devotion, so some lead to lamentation. [[9:23|and the multitude making a rout|et turbam tumultuantem]], that is, making a confused sound and a great din, talking, lamenting, and preparing what was needed for the funeral, [[9:24|He said: Give place|dicebat ad eos: Recedite]], going out of the house, and ceasing from this affliction and uproar; [[9:24|for the girl is not dead|non est enim puella mortua]] as far as I am concerned, though by the natural order she is dead, [[9:24|but sleepeth|sed dormit]] for Me, who can raise her from death more easily than you can wake a sleeper from sleep. So: She is not dead, that is, irreparably bereft of life, but sleeps, with the sleep of death, which is like the sleep of slumber. [[9:24|And they laughed him to scorn|Et deridebant eum]], [[Luke 8:53|knowing that she was dead|scientes quod mortua esset]]. For they were labouring under the ambiguity of the words, and did not understand the depth of Christ's words. And perhaps this girl was not dead with the death of guilt, though she was dead with the death of nature, so that this too is why it was said: She is not dead, but sleepeth.

paras.t: Et quum ejecta, id est de domo expulsa, esset turba tumultuans, quæ propter incredulitatem et derisionem Christi, digna non erat conspicere tantum miraculum, intravit cubiculum, et tenuit manum ejus, videlicet defuncta puellæ, dicens, imo, secundum Lucam, clamans: Puella, surge. Cui hoc dixit, jam non erat puella, sed cadaver seu corpus exanime. Anima quoque non surrexit localiter, nisi per accidens. Ponitur ergo pars pro toto. Corpori enim præcipitur ut resurgat. Et surrexit puella. In quo pensandum, quod non orando, sed imperando Christus puellam resuscitat: in quo ejus omnipotentia atque divinitas declarantur. Recolamus qualiter Elias et Eliseus mortuos suscitarunt, moxque sciemus quanta sit differentia in modo agendi illorum, et Christi, quamvis in facto convenientia quidam consistat. Illi ad Deum clamando, et super corpora exstineta ssæpius incumbendo, tandem impetrant quod deposcunt; iste solo imperio operatur quod placet. Quanta ergo differentia est inter Dominum imperantem, et servum orantem, tantum iste illos excedit.
paras.en: [[9:25|And when the multitude was put forth|Et quum ejecta, id est de domo expulsa, esset turba]], that is, driven out of the house, the multitude making the uproar, which, because of its unbelief and its mocking of Christ, was not worthy to see so great a miracle, [[9:25|he went in|intravit]] into the chamber, [[9:25|and took her by the hand|et tenuit manum ejus]], that is, the dead girl's, saying, or rather, according to Luke, crying out: [[Luke 8:54|Maid, arise|Puella, surge]]. The one to whom He said this was no longer a girl, but a corpse, that is, a lifeless body. Nor did the soul rise, in the sense of moving place, except incidentally. So the part is put for the whole: for it is the body that is commanded to rise. [[9:25|And the maid arose|Et surrexit puella]]. Here it is to be weighed that Christ raises the girl not by praying but by commanding, in which His almighty power and divinity are made plain. Let us call to mind how Elias and Eliseus raised the dead[[3 Kings 17:21||]][[4 Kings 4:33||]], and at once we shall know how great is the difference between their way of acting and Christ's, though there is a certain likeness in the deed. They, by crying to God and by lying again and again upon the dead bodies, at length obtained what they asked; He works what He pleases by His command alone. As great, then, as the difference between the Lord commanding and the servant praying, so far does He surpass them.

paras.t: Porro, secundum Lucam, nemo suscitationi puella interfuit, nisi Petrus, Jacobus et Joannes Christo familiarissimi, parentes quoque puellæ. Quamvis autem Salvator sine contactu potuerit illam reduxisse ad vitam, tenuit tamen manum ejus, ad ostendendum quod sua caro seu humanitas exstitit instrumentum unitæ ac operantis deitatis. Seeundum Marcum, puella resuscitata protinus ambulavit: quo viso, qui aderant obstupuerunt stupore maximo. Jesus vero vehementer eis præcepit, ut nemo hac sciret: jussitque puellæ dari cibaria; et comedit, ut veraciter suscitata probaretur. Quamvis autem Apostoli, et parentes puellæ tacuerunt, non vulgando miraculum istud, turba tamen ejecta, qua noverat puellam vere defunctam, percepto quod revixisset, non tacuit. Ideo subditur: Et exiit fama hæc, id est rumor tanti prodigii, in universam terram illam, hoc est ad omnes habitatores Galilææ, in qua facta sunt hæc.
paras.en: Moreover, according to Luke, no one was present at the raising of the girl except Peter, James and John, Christ's closest friends, and the girl's parents[[Luke 8:51||]]. And although the Saviour could have brought her back to life without touching her, He yet took her hand, to show that His flesh, that is, His humanity, was the instrument of the Godhead united to it and working through it. According to Mark, the girl, once raised, at once walked, and seeing this, those present [[Mark 5:42|were astonished with a great astonishment|obstupuerunt stupore maximo]]. But Jesus charged them strictly [[Mark 5:43|that no man should know it|ut nemo hæc sciret]], and ordered food to be given to the girl; and she ate, so that it might be proved that she was truly raised. But although the Apostles and the girl's parents kept silent and did not publish this miracle, yet the crowd that had been put out, which knew that the girl was really dead, when it learned that she had come back to life, did not keep silent. So it is added: [[9:26|And the fame hereof went abroad|Et exiit fama hæc]], that is, the report of so great a wonder, [[9:26|into all that country|in universam terram illam]], that is, to all the inhabitants of Galilee, in which these things were done.

paras.t: Denique tres mortuos legitur suscitasse Salvator, per quos spiritualis suscitatio trium generum hominum impiorum mystice figuratur. Suscitavit namque filiam Jairi in domo: per quod designatur spiritualis suscitatio eorum qui per peccatum interioris consensus, spiritualiter mortui sunt. Alium suscitavit in via ad tumulum, scilicet unicum filium viduæ: quo designatur spiritualiter suscitatio impiorum, propter peccatum operationis vita gratiæ destitutorum. Tertium suscitavit de monumento, utpote Lazarum: per quod figuratur spiritualis suscitatio habituatorum in malo, qui pessima consuetudine velut lapide grandi premuntur.
paras.en: Lastly, we read that the Saviour raised three dead persons, by whom is mystically figured the spiritual raising of three kinds of wicked men. For He raised the daughter of Jairus in the house: by which is signified the spiritual raising of those who are spiritually dead through the sin of inward consent. Another He raised on the way to the tomb, namely the only son of the widow[[Luke 7:12||]]: by which is signified the spiritual raising of the wicked who are bereft of the life of grace through the sin of deed. The third He raised from the tomb, namely Lazarus[[John 11:38||]]: by which is figured the spiritual raising of those who are hardened in evil by habit, who are weighed down by most evil custom as by a great stone.

paras.t: Specialiter vero per Jairum, qui interpretatur illuminans, quilibet bonus ac doctus prælatus, omnisque diligens propriæ animæ custos exprimitur. Quum ergo prælatus talis, seu homo timoratus, conspicit filiam suam, id est congregationem sibi commissam, seu propriam animam graviter infirmantem, pergat per desideria sancta ad Christum, eique procidens, oret pro spirituali sanatione hujusmodi filiæ, quatenus Christus per gratiæ infusionem, eam visitare, vivificare et salvare dignetur.
paras.en: In particular, by Jairus, whose name is interpreted 'enlightening', is signified every good and learned prelate, and everyone who diligently keeps watch over his own soul. When such a prelate, then, or a God-fearing man, sees his daughter, that is, the community entrusted to him, or his own soul, gravely sick, let him go by holy desires to Christ, and falling down before Him, let him pray for the spiritual healing of such a daughter, that Christ may deign to visit, quicken and save her by the infusion of grace.

paras.t: Et transeunte inde Jesu, id est, a domo archisynagogi eo redeunte, et patriam suam intrante, secundum Marcum, videlicet Nazareth, secundum Hieronymum, secuti sunt eum duo cæci ducti ab aliis, clamantes, et dicentes. Tamen clamor et dictio idem fuit in re, scilicet dictio seu locutio clamorosa ex magno affectu procedens. Miserere nostri, fili David, nostram cæcitatem tollendo, et nostræ miseriæ condolendo. Vocant autem eum filium David, quoniam crediderunt eum esse Christum, quem Judæi communiter noverant de semine David nasciturum.
paras.en: [[9:27|And as Jesus passed from thence|Et transeunte inde Jesu]], that is, from the house of the archisynagogue, as He went back and entered His own country, according to Mark[[Mark 6:1||]], namely Nazareth, according to Jerome, [[9:27|there followed him two blind men|secuti sunt eum duo cæci]], led by others, [[9:27|crying out and saying|clamantes, et dicentes]]. Yet the crying and the saying were in fact the same thing, namely a saying or speech uttered with a loud cry, coming from great feeling: [[9:27|Have mercy on us, O Son of David|Miserere nostri, fili David]], by taking away our blindness and pitying our misery. They call Him Son of David because they believed Him to be the Christ, whom the Jews commonly knew would be born of the seed of David.

paras.t: Quum autem Jesus venisset domum, id est ad suum hospitium: non enim habuit propriam domum, quia non habuit ubi caput reclinaret; accesserunt ad eum cæci. Et dicit eis Jesus. Creditis quia, id est quod, hoc, utpote lumen et visum oculorum, possum facere, id est tribuere, vobis? Non ex ignorantia sciscitatur, sed ut illi fideli oris confessione amplius mereantur, et ut manifestetur omnia possibilia esse perfecte credenti. Dicunt ei: Utique, Domine, credimus hoc. aliter non te essemus secuti.
paras.en: [[9:28|And when he was come to the house|Quum autem Jesus venisset domum]], that is, to His lodging (for He had no house of His own, since He [[Matt 8:20|hath not where to lay his head|non habuit ubi caput reclinaret]]), [[9:28|the blind men came to him|accesserunt ad eum cæci]]. [[9:28|And Jesus saith to them, Do you believe, that I can do this unto you?|Et dicit eis Jesus: Creditis quia hoc possum facere vobis?]] 'This', that is, the light and sight of the eyes; 'do', that is, give. He asks not out of ignorance, but that by the confession of their mouths they might merit more, and that it might be made known that [[Mark 9:22|all things are possible to him that believeth|omnia possibilia esse perfecte credenti]]. [[9:28|They say to him, Yea, Lord|Dicunt ei: Utique, Domine]], we believe this; otherwise we should not have followed You.

paras.t: Tunc tetigit oculos eorum, dicens: Secundum fidem vestram, id est, prout credidistis, et juxta exigentiam meriti fidei vestræ, fiat vobis, hoc est, recipiatis quod creditis vobis posse conferri a me. Et aperti sunt oculi eorum corporales, proprio actu utendo. Et comminatus, id est cum minis locutus, est eis Jesus dicens cum imperio, quoniam mala eis minabatur, nisi obedirent suo præcepto, quo ait: Videte, id est quantum in vobis est cavete, ne quis absentium sciat istud miraculum. Illi autem exeuntes de domo in qua visum receperunt, diffamaverunt, id est, diversimode atque celebriter famaverunt seu famosum fecerunt, eum, a quo tantum beneficium erant sortiti, in tota terra illa Galilææ.
paras.en: [[9:29|Then he touched their eyes, saying, According to your faith, be it done unto you|Tunc tetigit oculos eorum, dicens: Secundum fidem vestram, fiat vobis]]: that is, as you have believed, and as the merit of your faith requires, receive what you believe can be given you by Me. [[9:30|And their eyes were opened|Et aperti sunt oculi eorum]], their bodily eyes, so as to use their own act. [[9:30|and Jesus strictly charged them|Et comminatus, id est cum minis locutus, est eis Jesus]], that is, spoke to them with threats, [[9:30|saying|dicens]] with command, since He threatened them with evil unless they obeyed His precept, in which He says: [[9:30|See|Videte]], that is, take care as far as in you lies, [[9:30|that no man know this|ne quis absentium sciat]], none of those absent, this miracle. [[9:31|But they going out|Illi autem exeuntes]] of the house in which they received their sight, [[9:31|spread his fame abroad|diffamaverunt eum]], that is, made Him famous in many ways and widely, Him from whom they had received so great a benefit, [[9:31|in all that country|in tota terra illa]] of Galilee.

paras.t: Quæritur, an hoc agendo bene fecerunt. Videtur quod imo, quoniam ex magnitudine devotionis et gratitudinis hoc fecerunt. Apparet tamen quod non, eo quod Christo non obedierunt. Et respondendum, quod omnis Christi actio, nostra est instructio. Interdum ergo Christus præcepit vel permisit miracula sua manifestari, ad gloriam Dei et hominum ædificationem, seu fidei confirmationem, ut instrueret nos quod vicissim debeamus simili ratione propria bona aliis propalare, juxta illud: Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus. Unde et Paulus virtutes suas et signa diligenter describit, in tantum ut dicat: Nihil minus feci ab his qui sunt supra modum Apostoli. Aliquando vero Salvator jussit sua miracula occultari, ut doceat nos hominum laudes et admirationes omnemque vanitatem abhorrere ac fugere. Illi vero qui nihilo minus ejus miracula ad Dei gloriam predicaverunt, dicuntur non fecisse contra Christi præceptum, quia præceptum ejus intelligebatur secundum unam considerationem, videlicet, ne talia signa panderentur ex vanitate propter jactantiam, et etiam ut per tale præceptum doceremur vanam gloriam abjicere. Voluit tamen ea manifestari propter alias rationes jam introductas. Idem autem secundum diversos respectus est volitum, et non volitum. Sic ergo cæci illustrati mente magis quam corpore, impleverunt secundum quosdam, Christi præceptum, quoad verum intellectum ipsius.
paras.en: It is asked whether in doing this they did well. It seems that they did, since they did it from the greatness of their devotion and gratitude. Yet it appears that they did not, because they did not obey Christ. And it must be answered that every action of Christ is our instruction. Sometimes, then, Christ commanded or allowed His miracles to be made known, for the glory of God and the edification of men, that is, the confirming of faith, to teach us that we in turn ought for a like reason to make our own good things known to others, according to that saying: [[Matt 5:16|let your light shine before men|Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus]]. Whence Paul too carefully describes his virtues and signs, so far as to say: [[2 Cor 12:11|I have no way come short of them that are above measure apostles|Nihil minus feci ab his qui sunt supra modum Apostoli]]. But sometimes the Saviour ordered His miracles to be hidden, to teach us to shrink from and flee the praises and admiration of men and all vanity. Those, however, who none the less proclaimed His miracles to the glory of God are said not to have acted against Christ's command, because His command was understood under one consideration, namely, that such signs should not be spread abroad out of vanity, for boasting, and also that by such a command we should be taught to cast away vainglory. Yet He willed them to be made known for the other reasons already given. And the same thing, under different respects, is willed and not willed. So these blind men, enlightened in mind more than in body, fulfilled Christ's command, according to some, as to its true meaning.

paras.t: Egressis autem illis duobus cæcis jam illuminatis, de domo in qua illuminati sunt a lumine luminum, ecce qui aderant, obtulerunt ei, videlicet Christo, hominem mutum, dæmonium habentem, id est possessum a dæmone ipsum mutificante. Non enim hic homo mutus erat ex naturali defectu, sed dæmonis operatione, usum linguæ in eo impedientis. Quemadmodum namque dæmones loqui possunt per homines a se obsessos idiomata talibus hominibus prorsus ignota, movendo linguas eorum ad talium prolationem verborum, eo quod natura corporalis obediat spirituali substantiæ, quantum ad motum localem, ut Thomas pulchre declarat; sic impedire possunt organa corporis humani ab actibus suis, videlicet linguam a loquela, sicque efficiunt hominem mutum. Et ejecto dæmonio, quod Christus ab homine expulit potenti imperio, quoniam omnia subjecta erant pedibus suis, locutus est mutus, id est, qui mutus exstiterat. Cessante enim causa, cessat effectus. Et ideo sicut dæmon per suam præsentiam fecit hominem mutum, sic per suam expulsionem, restitutus est homo pristinæ facultati loquendi.
paras.en: [[9:32|And when they were gone out|Egressis autem illis]], those two blind men now given light, from the house in which they were enlightened by the Light of lights, [[9:32|behold they brought him a dumb man, possessed with a devil|ecce … obtulerunt ei … hominem mutum, dæmonium habentem]], that is, Christ; they who were there brought a man possessed by a demon that made him dumb. For this man was not dumb from a natural defect, but by the working of a demon hindering the use of his tongue. For just as demons can speak, through men possessed by them, languages wholly unknown to such men, by moving their tongues to utter such words, because bodily nature obeys spiritual substance as to local motion, as Thomas finely explains, so they can hinder the organs of the human body from their acts, namely the tongue from speech, and so make a man dumb. [[9:33|And after the devil was cast out|Et ejecto dæmonio]], which Christ drove out of the man by His powerful command, since [[Ps 8:8|all things under his feet|omnia subjecta erant pedibus suis]] were subject, [[9:33|the dumb man spoke|locutus est mutus]], that is, he who had been dumb. For when the cause ceases, the effect ceases. And so, just as the demon by his presence made the man dumb, so by his expulsion the man was restored to his former power of speech.

paras.t: Et admiratæ sunt turbæ, propter insolitum opus. Imo duo signa in eodem peracta sunt, videlicet dæmonis ejectio, et linguæ relaxatio. Multoque amplius admirabilis, virtuosus et gloriosus fuit modus agendi, quam opus, scilicet, quod tam imperialiter atque faciliter, et item tam frequenter et quasi innumerabiliter Christus signa ista peregit. Ideo admiratæ sunt turbæ, dicentes: Nunquam apparuit sic in Israel, id est, nunquam aliquis Israelita, Patriarcha sive Propheta, tam gloriose operatus est, ut iste. Quamvis enim multi eorum fecerint signa majora, quam sit dæmonem mutum expellere, sicut Josue et Isaias, ad quorum instantiam sol a naturali cursu cessavit; nullus tamen in veteri Testamento, tot et tanta fecit miracula, tamque potenter et imperialiter, sieut Christus. Propter quod in Joanne dicit: Si opera non fecissem in eis, qua nemo alius fecit, peccatum non haberent.
paras.en: [[9:33|and the multitudes wondered|Et admiratæ sunt turbæ]], at the unaccustomed work. Indeed two signs were done in the same man, namely the casting out of the demon and the loosing of the tongue. And much more wonderful, mighty and glorious than the work was the manner of working, namely that Christ did these signs so commandingly and so easily, and also so often and almost without number. Therefore [[9:33|the multitudes wondered, saying, Never was the like seen in Israel|admiratæ sunt turbæ, dicentes: Nunquam apparuit sic in Israel]], that is, never has any Israelite, Patriarch or Prophet worked so gloriously as this man. For although many of them did greater signs than driving out a dumb demon, as Josue and Isaias, at whose request the sun stopped its natural course[[Jos 10:12||]][[Is 38:8||]], yet no one in the Old Testament did so many and such great miracles, and so mightily and commandingly, as Christ. For which reason He says in John: [[John 15:24|If I had not done among them the works that no other man hath done, they would not have sin|Si opera non fecissem in eis, qua nemo alius fecit, peccatum non haberent]].

paras.t: Pharisæi autem, qui erant ambitiosi, avari, et invidi, maxime contra Christum, quia eorum vitia increpabat liberrime, dicebant, ex invidia rationis judicium obtenebrante. Amor enim privatus et odium pervertunt judicium, juxta illud Prophetæ: Numquid vestrum est scire judicium, qui odio habetis bonum? In principe dæmoniorum, id est virtute et cooperatione pessimi dæmonis, huie seductori familia: ris, eum quo pactum habet, ejicit dæmones ab obsessis, ita quod ejectio dæmonum est obedientia in suum superiorem, ad cujus invocationem iste dæmonia ejicit. Dicebant itaque, quod Jesus principi dæmoniorum, videlicet Beelzebub, esset concors et familiaris, et quod dæmon ille superior præciperet dæmonibus inferioribus exire ab hominibus ad invocationem seu imperium Jesu, quatenus homines æstimantes talia fieri potestate divina, seducerentur, putando Jesum esse Christum sive prophetam. Sic quoque dicebant miracula Salvatoris fieri magicis artibus. Falsitatem vero hujus dicti Christus infra evidenter ostendit, sicut patebit.
paras.en: [[9:34|But the Pharisees|Pharisæi autem]], who were ambitious, greedy and envious, above all against Christ, because He rebuked their vices most freely, [[9:34|said|dicebant]], out of envy darkening the judgement of reason. For private love and hatred pervert judgement, according to that saying of the Prophet: [[Mich 3:1|Is it not your part to know judgment|Numquid vestrum est scire judicium]], [[Mich 3:2|You that hate good|qui odio habetis bonum]]? [[9:34|By the prince of devils|In principe dæmoniorum]], that is, by the power and co-operation of the worst demon, who is familiar to this seducer and with whom he has a pact, [[9:34|he casteth out devils|ejicit dæmones]] from the possessed; so that the casting out of the demons is obedience to their superior, at whose invocation this man casts out demons. So they said that Jesus was in league and familiar with the prince of demons, namely Beelzebub, and that that higher demon commanded the lower demons to go out of men at the invocation or command of Jesus, so that men, thinking such things were done by divine power, might be led astray, taking Jesus for the Christ or a prophet. So too they said that the Saviour's miracles were done by magic arts. The falsity of this saying Christ shows plainly below[[Matt 12:25||]], as will appear.

paras.t: Et circuibat Jesus cum discipulis suis, civitates omnes et castella Galilææ et aliarum terrarum vicinarum, et simpliciter omnes civitates et castella, vel quasdam de omnibus, ut sit distributio pro generibus singulorum. Vel forte est locutio hyperbolica, id est per excessum prolata, ad insinuandum quod valde multa loca circuivit. Docens in synagogis eorum, videlicet Judeorum, ad quas convenire solebant ut audirent verbum Dei. Porro, per hoc quod Christus non solum civitates, sed et castella circuivit, docentur prelati et predicatores, non postponere curam paucorum, et eorum qui in parvis locis morantur, sed omnibus et singulis pro viribus providere. Et prædicans evangelium regni, id est evangelicam legem atque doctrinam, in qua regnum cæleste promittitur, et per cujus observantiam ad illud directe ac immediate pertingitur, et curans omnem languorem graviorem, et omnem infirmitatem minorem. Vel languor refertur ad vitia animæ, infirmitas autem ad incommoda corporis. Nam quos curavit in corpore, sanavit quoque in anima. Primo itaque prædicavit et docuit; deinde ægritudines repulit, quatenus operatio miraculorum supernaturalem doctrinam commendaret, auditoribusque vehementer infigeret, et ut eos quos sermo non emendavit, signa converterent.
paras.en: [[9:35|And Jesus went about all the cities and towns|Et circuibat Jesus cum discipulis suis, civitates omnes et castella]] with His disciples, of Galilee and of other neighbouring lands; and simply all the cities and towns, or some of all of them, so that it is a distribution by kinds of individuals [that is, 'all' means some of every kind, not every single one]. Or perhaps it is a hyperbolic expression, that is, said by way of excess, to suggest that He went round a great many places. [[9:35|teaching in their synagogues|Docens in synagogis eorum]], that is, of the Jews, where they used to gather to hear the word of God. Further, by the fact that Christ went round not only the cities but also the towns [castella: villages and small walled places], prelates and preachers are taught not to put aside the care of the few, and of those who live in small places, but to provide for each and all as far as they can. [[9:35|and preaching the gospel of the kingdom|Et prædicans evangelium regni]], that is, the Gospel law and teaching, in which the heavenly kingdom is promised, and by the keeping of which one reaches it directly and immediately, [[9:35|and healing every disease|et curans omnem languorem]], the graver, [[9:35|and every infirmity|et omnem infirmitatem]], the lesser. Or 'disease' refers to the vices of the soul, 'infirmity' to the ills of the body. For those He cured in body He healed also in soul. So He first preached and taught, then drove away sicknesses, so that the working of miracles might commend His supernatural teaching and fix it deeply in His hearers, and so that signs might convert those whom the word had not amended.

paras.t: Frequenter Evangelistæ describunt Christi miracula in communi, nam tot, tanta, et talia exstiterunt, quod sigillatim et plene recitari non poterant: in quo evidenter ostenditur virtus et veritas Christi, præsertim quum nil tale legatur de aliquo Sancto veteris Testamenti, quamvis Elias et Eliseus plurima fecerint signa. Hinc Joannes ait: Multa quidem alia fecit Jesus, quæ si scribantur per singula, nec ipsum arbitror mundum capere posse eos qui scribendi sunt libros.
paras.en: The Evangelists often describe Christ's miracles in general, for they were so many, so great and of such a kind that they could not be related one by one and in full: in which the power and truth of Christ is plainly shown, especially since nothing of the kind is read of any Saint of the Old Testament, although Elias and Eliseus did very many signs. Hence John says: [[John 21:25|many other things which Jesus did; which, if they were written every one, the world itself, I think, would not be able to contain the books that should be written|Multa quidem alia fecit Jesus, quæ si scribantur per singula, nec ipsum arbitror mundum capere posse eos qui scribendi sunt libros]].

paras.t: Videns autem Jesus turbas ipsum sequentes, misertus est eis, tanquam misericordissimus et amator præcipuus; quia erant vexati lassitudine, fame, siti, et etiam dolore cordis propter commissa mala et bona omissa: de quibus cordialiter multi eorum poanitebant, ex. verbis Christi ad compunctionem inducti; et jacentes præ fatigatione: et forte jacebant in terra sub dio, carentes hospitio, quoniam plures eorum pauperes erant, nec poterant præ multitudine faciliter hospitari, et illum sequebantur qui personaliter non habebat reclinatorium capitis. Erant ergo afflicti sicut oves non habentes pastorem: quoniam sicut oves tales non habent alentem, et eas in stabulum colligentem, ne devorentur a lupis; sic isti carebant bonis doctoribus ac prælatis, excepto Christo et ejus discipulis. Sacerdotes quippe et Scribæ pascebant et quærebant se ipsos, non gregem sibi commissum. De talibus enim Dominus dicit per Prophetam: Qui comederunt carnem populi mei, et pellem desuper excoriaverunt. Et per Jeremiam: Sacerdotes, inquit, non dixerunt, Ubi est Dominus? et tenentes legem nescierunt me; et pastores prævaricati sunt in me. Sed quum Christus sit pastor bonus, quomodo gregem se sequentem comparat ovibus sine pastore? Et respondendum, quod excepit semetipsum. Vel ideo dicit eum similem ovibus sine pastore, quoniam licet ipse in spiritualibus pasceret se sequentes, non tamen semper in temporalibus seu corporalibus, sed erant sæpe in magna penuria.
paras.en: [[9:36|And seeing the multitudes|Videns autem Jesus turbas]] that followed Him, [[9:36|he had compassion on them|misertus est eis]], as most merciful and their great lover; [[9:36|because they were distressed|quia erant vexati]] with weariness, hunger, thirst, and also grief of heart for the evil they had done and the good they had left undone, for which many of them repented from the heart, brought to compunction by Christ's words; [[9:36|and lying|et jacentes]] from fatigue: and perhaps they lay on the ground under the open sky, without lodging, since many of them were poor, nor could they easily be lodged because of their numbers, and they were following Him who in His own person had nowhere to lay His head[[Matt 8:20||]]. They were afflicted, then, [[9:36|like sheep that have no shepherd|sicut oves non habentes pastorem]]: for as such sheep have no one to feed them and to gather them into the fold lest they be devoured by wolves, so these lacked good teachers and prelates, apart from Christ and His disciples. For the priests and scribes fed and sought themselves, not the flock entrusted to them. Of such the Lord says through the Prophet: [[Mich 3:3|Who have eaten the flesh of my people, and have flayed their skin off them|Qui comederunt carnem populi mei, et pellem desuper excoriaverunt]]. And through Jeremias: [[Jer 2:8|The priests did not say: Where is the Lord? and they that held the law knew me not, and the pastors transgressed against me|Sacerdotes … non dixerunt … prævaricati sunt in me]]. But since Christ is the [[John 10:11|good shepherd|pastor bonus]], how does He compare the flock following Him to sheep without a shepherd? It must be answered that He excepted Himself. Or He says they are like sheep without a shepherd because, although He fed those following Him in spiritual things, He did not always do so in temporal or bodily things, but they were often in great want.

paras.t: Tunc Christus providus pastor dicit discipulis suis: Messis quidem multa, id est, multi sunt parati audire et facere verba Dei: qui messi comparantur, quia dispositi sunt congregari ac recipi in horreum Christi, tanquam boni fructus, et in virtute maturi. De talibus enim ait Joannes Baptista, loquens de Christo: Triticum colliget in horreum suum, videlicet in Ecclesiam militantem et triumphantem. Operarii autem, id est boni et efficaces pastores, doctores ac prædicatores, sunt pauci, imo paucissimi, et tanto pauciores, quanto major perfectio requiritur ad bonum pastorem, qui verbo et opere congreget populum in domum seu horreum Dei. Nam et si sint qui audiant, desunt qui dicant. Rogate ergo Dominum messis, videlicet Christum, omnium hominum dominatorem, seu Deum Trinitatem, Dominum universorum, maxime electorum, in quibus actualiter dominatur, dum ei obediunt, ut mittat operarios, id est fructuosos atque idoneos doctores et prælatos, in messem suam, id est ad plebem Ecclesiæ instruendam ac gubernandam. Maximum etenim Dei beneficium est, habere bonum pastorem, quoniam vere ait Scriptura: Qualis est rector civitatis, tales et habitantes in ea. Hoc Moyses oravit, dicens: Provideat Dominus Deus spirituum universæ carnis, hominem qui sit super multitudinem hanc, ne sit populus Domini sicut oves sine pastore. Tales operarios promittit se Dominus præstiturum per Jeremiam prophetam, dicens: Dabo vobis pastores juxta cor meum, et pascent vos scientia et doctrina. Ecclesia ergo, quæ secundum Apostolum, est Dei agricultura, et secundum Isaiam, dicitur vinea Domini, ipsa quoque nunc dicitur messis Domini.
paras.en: [[9:37|Then he saith to his disciples|Tunc dicit discipulis suis]], Christ the provident shepherd: [[9:37|The harvest indeed is great|Messis quidem multa]], that is, many are ready to hear and do the words of God, who are compared to a harvest because they are disposed to be gathered and received into Christ's barn, as good fruits ripe in virtue. Of such John the Baptist says, speaking of Christ: and will [[Matt 3:12|gather his wheat into the barn|Triticum colliget in horreum suum]], namely into the Church militant and triumphant. [[9:37|but the labourers|Operarii autem]], that is, good and effective pastors, teachers and preachers, [[9:37|are few|pauci]], indeed very few, and the fewer as greater perfection is required for a good pastor, who by word and deed should gather the people into the house or barn of God. For even if there are those who would hear, there are not those to speak. [[9:38|Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest|Rogate ergo Dominum messis]], namely Christ, the ruler of all men, or God the Trinity, the Lord of all things, above all of the elect, in whom He rules in act while they obey Him, [[9:38|that he send forth labourers|ut mittat operarios]], that is, fruitful and fit teachers and prelates, [[9:38|into his harvest|in messem suam]], that is, to instruct and govern the people of the Church. For it is a very great benefit of God to have a good pastor, since Scripture truly says: [[Ecclus 10:2|what manner of man the ruler of a city is, such also are they that dwell therein|Qualis est rector civitatis, tales et habitantes in ea]]. This Moses prayed for, saying: [[Num 27:16|May the Lord the God of the spirits of all flesh provide a man, that may be over this multitude|Provideat Dominus Deus spirituum universæ carnis, hominem qui sit super multitudinem hanc]], [[Num 27:17|lest the people of the Lord be as sheep without a shepherd|ne sit populus Domini sicut oves sine pastore]]. Such labourers the Lord promises to give through the prophet Jeremias, saying: [[Jer 3:15|And I will give you pastors according to my own heart, and they shall feed you with knowledge and doctrine|Dabo vobis pastores juxta cor meum, et pascent vos scientia et doctrina]]. So the Church, which according to the Apostle is [[1 Cor 3:9|God's husbandry|Dei agricultura]], and according to Isaias is called [[Is 5:7|the vineyard of the Lord|vinea Domini]], is now called also the harvest of the Lord.

10.title: Elucidatio capituli decimi: Et convocatis duodecim discipulis suis, dedit illis potestatem, etc.
10.title_en: Explanation of the tenth chapter: “And having called his twelve disciples together, he gave them power”, etc.

paras.t: Postquam Christus docuit se rogandum ut mitteret operarios in messem suam, statim, nondum rogatus, saltem condigne, ex abundantia suæ clementiæ mittit operarios sanctos Apostolos in messem suam, de qua alio asserit loco: Non sum missus nisi ad oves qua perierunt domus Israel. Itaque, postquam instruxit Apostolos de evangelicæ legis doctrina, multisque miraculis eos confirmavit in fide, mittit eos ut alios doceant. Ut enim Dionysius protestatur, non est aptus alios ad Deum reducere, purgando, illuminando, perficiendoque eos, nisi qui in se ipso excellenter purgatus, illuminatus, perfectusque fuerit, quatenus de plenitudine ejus accipiant alii.
paras.en: After Christ had taught that He must be asked to send labourers into His harvest, at once, not yet asked, or at least not worthily, out of the abundance of His mercy He sends the holy Apostles as labourers into His harvest, of which He says in another place: [[Matt 15:24|I was not sent but to the sheep, that are lost of the house of Israel|Non sum missus nisi ad oves qua perierunt domus Israel]]. So, after He had instructed the Apostles in the teaching of the Gospel law and had confirmed them in the faith by many miracles, He sends them to teach others. For, as Dionysius declares, no one is fit to lead others back to God, by purifying, enlightening and perfecting them, unless he has himself been excellently purified, enlightened and perfected, so that others may receive of his fulness[[John 1:16||]].

paras.t: Et convocatis duodecim discipulis suis, puta Apostolis, ad se, dedit illis Jesus potestatem spirituum immundorum, id est virtutem supra et contra dæmones impuritate peccati repletos, ut ejicerent eos ab hominibus obsessis, in nomine Christi. Dedit quoque eis potestatem, ut ut curarent omnem languorem difficulter sanabilem, inveteratum, latentem, et omnem infirmitatem facilius curabilem, hoc est omne genus cujuscumque morbi. Vel per languorem, invaletudo animæ seu peccatum, per infirmitatem vero, morbus corporis designatur. Nam et corporum curatio ordinabatur ad animæ sanationem: de qua Jeremias, Sana me (inquit) et sanabor. Missi sunt ergo Apostoli ad animas reparandas. Data præterea est Apostolis tanta miraculorum potestas, quatenus veritas evangelicæ pradicationis divino testimonio fulciretur, et quia non aliter crederetur illitteratis ac idiotis.
paras.en: [[10:1|And having called his twelve disciples together|Et convocatis duodecim discipulis suis]], that is, the Apostles, to Himself, Jesus [[10:1|gave them power over unclean spirits|dedit illis Jesus potestatem spirituum immundorum]], that is, power over and against demons filled with the uncleanness of sin, [[10:1|to cast them out|ut ejicerent eos]] of men possessed, in the name of Christ. He also gave them power [[10:1|to heal all manner of diseases|ut curarent omnem languorem]], those hard to heal, long-standing, hidden, [[10:1|and all manner of infirmities|et omnem infirmitatem]] more easily curable, that is, every kind of any sickness whatever. Or by 'disease' is meant the ill-health of the soul, that is, sin, and by 'infirmity' the sickness of the body. For the curing of bodies too was ordered to the healing of the soul, of which Jeremias says: [[Jer 17:14|Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed|Sana me (inquit) et sanabor]]. So the Apostles were sent to repair souls. Moreover, so great a power of miracles was given to the Apostles so that the truth of the Gospel preaching might be supported by divine testimony, and because otherwise unlettered and simple men would not be believed.

paras.t: Duodecim autem Apostolorum nomina sunt hæc. Ponit Evangelista nomina Apostolorum, ne alii pseudoapostoli reciperentur quasi veri Apostoli. Ut enim in epistolis Pauli frequenter ostenditur, tempore Apostolorum, multi falsi apostoli surrexerunt, dicentes se veros Christi Apostolos. Primus dignitate, non vocatione, est Simon, qui alio nomine dicitur Petrus, et etiam Cephas. Simon autem fuit primum nomen ipsius: alia duo nomina imposuit illi Christus. Simon interpretatur obediens; Petrus, firmus; Cephas, caput, vel principalis. Petrus tamen et Cephas idem significant, ita quod Petrus interpretatur firmus et principalis, similiter Cephas. Unde alio in loco ait Salvator: Tu vocaberis Cephas, quod interpretatur Petrus. Et Andreas frater ejus, videlicet Petri. Quamvis autem Petrus et Andreas primo simul a Christo vocati sint ad apostolatum, ut dictum est supra, Andreas tamen primo a Christo vocatus est ad sui cognitionem, et cognito Christo, Andreas duxit fratrem suum Petrum ipso seniorem, ad Christum.
paras.en: [[10:2|And the names of the twelve Apostles are these|Duodecim autem Apostolorum nomina sunt hæc]]. The Evangelist gives the names of the Apostles so that other, false apostles should not be received as true Apostles. For, as is often shown in the epistles of Paul[[2 Cor 11:13||]][[Gal 1:7||]], in the time of the Apostles many false apostles arose, calling themselves true Apostles of Christ. [[10:2|The first|Primus]] in dignity, not in calling, is [[10:2|Simon who is called Peter|Simon, qui alio nomine dicitur Petrus]], and also Cephas. Simon was his first name; the other two names Christ gave him[[Matt 16:18||]]. Simon is interpreted 'obedient'; Peter, 'firm'; Cephas, 'head', or 'chief'. Yet Peter and Cephas mean the same, so that Peter is interpreted 'firm' and 'chief', and likewise Cephas. Whence in another place the Saviour says: [[John 1:42|Thou shalt be called Cephas, which is interpreted Peter|Tu vocaberis Cephas, quod interpretatur Petrus]]. [[10:2|and Andrew his brother|Et Andreas frater ejus]], that is, Peter's. For although Peter and Andrew were first called together by Christ to the apostolate, as was said above[[Matt 4:18||]], yet Andrew was first called by Christ to know Him[[John 1:40||]], and having come to know Christ, Andrew brought his brother Peter, who was older than he, to Christ[[John 1:42||]].

paras.t: Jacobus Major, id est vocatione prior, et Christo familiarior: qui interfuit resuscitationi puellæ, Transfigurationi, et trinæ orationi Christi tempore passionis; Zebedæi filius, et Joannes evangelista, frater ejus, utpote Jacobi. Hos duos, ut Marcus refert, Christus vocavit Boanerges, id est Filios tonitrui, propter altisonam et invictam Evangelii prædicationem. Philippus: quem Christus legitur apud Joannem statim post suam baptizationem vocasse. Eratque Philippus a Bethsaida, et frater Nathanaelis de quo testatus est Christus: Ecce vere Israelita, in quo dolus non est. Et Bartholomæus; Thomas, et Matthæus publicanus. Lucas et Marcus nominant Matthæum ante Thomam, nec addunt, Publicanus. Matthæus vero sicut vere humilis, Thomam sibi præponit, seque publicanum appellat. Et Jacobus Minor, filius Alphæi; qui dictus est frater Domini, tanquam vultu et conversatione ei conformis; et fuit primus Jerosolymorum Christianorum antistes; et Thaddæus: qui aliis in locis vocatur Judas Jacobi, id est frater Jacobi Minoris; qui etiam, teste Hieronymo, dicebatur Lebbæus, quod interpretatur corculus, id est cordis sui diligens custos. Fuit ergo trinomius.
paras.en: [[10:3|James|Jacobus]] the Greater, that is, the earlier in calling and the more familiar with Christ, who was present at the raising of the girl[[Mark 5:37||]], at the Transfiguration[[Matt 17:1||]], and at Christ's threefold prayer in the time of His passion[[Mark 14:33||]]; [[10:3|the son of Zebedee, and John his brother|Zebedæi filius, et Joannes evangelista, frater ejus]], John the Evangelist, the brother of James. These two, as Mark relates, Christ called [[Mark 3:17|Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder|Boanerges, id est Filios tonitrui]], because of their lofty and unconquered preaching of the Gospel. [[10:3|Philip|Philippus]], whom Christ is read in John to have called immediately after His baptism[[John 1:43||]]. And Philip was from Bethsaida[[John 1:44||]], and the brother of Nathanael, of whom Christ testified: [[John 1:47|Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile|Ecce vere Israelita, in quo dolus non est]]. [[10:3|and Bartholomew, Thomas and Matthew the publican|Et Bartholomæus; Thomas, et Matthæus publicanus]]. Luke and Mark name Matthew before Thomas[[Luke 6:15||]][[Mark 3:18||]], and do not add 'the publican'. But Matthew, as one truly humble, puts Thomas before himself and calls himself a publican. [[10:3|and James the son of Alpheus|Et Jacobus Minor, filius Alphæi]], the Less, who was called the brother of the Lord[[Gal 1:19||]], as being like Him in face and manner of life; and he was the first bishop of the Christians of Jerusalem; [[10:3|and Thaddeus|et Thaddæus]], who in other places is called Jude of James, that is, the brother of James the Less[[Luke 6:16||]][[Acts 1:13||]]; who also, as Jerome testifies, was called Lebbeus, which is interpreted 'little heart' [corculus], that is, a careful keeper of his heart. So he had three names.

paras.t: Simon Cananæus: qui dicitur Cananeus, non quia de genere populi Chanaan, sed a vico Cana, ubi Christus convertit aquam in vinum. Hunc Lucas vocat Simonem Zelotem, quoniam Cana interpretatur zelus, secundum Hieronymum. Et Judas Iscariotes, id est natus a vico Judææ nomine Carioth, qui et tradidit eum, videlicet Jesum, dicens: Quid vultis mihi dare, et ego eum vobis tradam? Qui velut alter Lucifer cecidit de cœlo, et tanquam alter Satan adfuit inter filios Dei.
paras.en: [[10:4|Simon the Cananean|Simon Cananæus]]: who is called the Cananean, not because he was of the race of the people of Chanaan, but from the village of Cana, where Christ turned water into wine[[John 2:1||]]. Luke calls him Simon Zelotes[[Luke 6:15||]], because Cana is interpreted 'zeal', according to Jerome. [[10:4|and Judas Iscariot|Et Judas Iscariotes]], that is, born in a village of Judea named Carioth, [[10:4|who also betrayed him|qui et tradidit eum]], that is, Jesus, saying: [[Matt 26:15|What will you give me, and I will deliver him unto you?|Quid vultis mihi dare, et ego eum vobis tradam?]] Who, like another Lucifer, fell from heaven[[Is 14:12||]], and like another Satan was present among the sons of God[[Job 1:6||]].

paras.t: Hos duodecim misit Jesus ad prædicandum, binos et binos, seu combinatos, secundum Marcum. Unde quod Matthæus et Lucas exprimunt eos combinatos, putant nonnulli ideo factum, quia illi pariter missi sunt, qui combinantur. Denique post hanc missionem Apostolorum, designavit Dominus Jesus et alios septuaginta duos discipulos, et misit illos binos et binos ante faciem suam, ut Lucas refert. Præcipiens eis, puta Apostolis, et dicens: In viam gentium, id est ducentem ad gentiles, ne abieritis, eos visitando seu instruendo, et in civitates Samaritanorum: qui rcœperunt quinque libros Moysis, sed non Prophetas; erantque natione gentiles, et a rege Assyriorum adducti, filiis Israel captis, prout in libris Regum plenius edocetur; ne intraveritis, gratia prædicandi, nec in villas aut castella eorum.
paras.en: [[10:5|These twelve Jesus sent|Hos duodecim misit Jesus]] to preach, two and two, that is, paired, according to Mark[[Mark 6:7||]]. Hence, because Matthew and Luke set them out in pairs[[Luke 6:14||]], some think this was done because those who are paired were sent together. Then after this sending of the Apostles, [[Luke 10:1|the Lord appointed also other seventy-two. And he sent them two and two before his face|designavit Dominus … binos et binos … ante faciem suam]], as Luke relates. [[10:5|commanding them, saying|Præcipiens eis, puta Apostolis, et dicens]], that is, the Apostles: [[10:5|Go ye not into the way of the Gentiles|In viam gentium ne abieritis]], that is, the way leading to the Gentiles, visiting or instructing them, [[10:5|and into the city of the Samaritans|et in civitates Samaritanorum]], who received the five books of Moses but not the Prophets, and were Gentiles by nation, brought in by the king of the Assyrians when the children of Israel had been taken captive, as is taught more fully in the books of Kings[[4 Kings 17:24||]], [[10:5|enter ye not|ne intraveritis]] for the sake of preaching, nor into their villages or towns.

paras.t: Sed potius ad oves quæ perierunt, id est perditas, seu propter peccatum damnationi obnoxias, domus, id est populi seu familiæ Israel. Potest autem per Israel intelligi Jacob patriarcha, de quo Judæi exorti sunt, qui alio nomine nuncupatus est Israel; vel populus Israeliticus.
paras.en: [[10:6|But go ye rather to the lost sheep|Sed potius ad oves quæ perierunt]], that is, lost, or liable to damnation on account of sin, [[10:6|of the house of Israel|domus Israël]], that is, of the people or family of Israel. By Israel may be understood the patriarch Jacob, from whom the Jews sprang, who by another name was called Israel[[Gen 32:28||]]; or the people of Israel.

paras.t: Quemadmodum ergo Christus ait, Non sum missus nisi ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel; sic et Apostolos mittit solum ad illas: non quod ipse nullo modo missus sit ad gentes, præsertim quum in Actibus Apostolorum dicat Apostolus, Notum vobis sit, quia gentibus missum est hoc salutare Dei; et Simeon justus, Viderunt, inquit, oculi mei Salutare tuum, quod parasti ante faciem omnium populorum. Sed quoniam primo ac principaliter missus est ad convertendos Judæos, deinde gentiles; sic nunc jubentur Apostoli solis prædicare Judæis: quoniam primo eis prædicari decebat tanquam populo peculiari, quorum patres ex quibus Christus, ad quos facta fuit de Christi adventu promissio; et etiam ut Judæi inexcusabiles fierent de sua incredulitate. Si enim Christus suos discipulos ad infideles primo misisset, habuissent occasionem calumniandi atque dicendi, quod ipse non esset Christus in lege promissus populo Judæorum. Itaque, quoniam Christus et ejus discipuli ante passionem ipsius modico tempore prædicaverunt, idcirco ante passionem non prædicaverunt nisi Judæis. Porro, post resurrectionem dixit eis Salvator: Euntes in mundum universum, prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ. Et tamen nec hoc exsecuti sunt Apostoli, nisi post prædicationem Judæis copiose et diu impensam: quibus pro majori parte induratis, ad gentes profecti sunt. Propter quod Paulus et Barnabas dixerunt Judæis: Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei, sed quoniam repulistis illud, ecce convertimur ad gentes.
paras.en: As, then, Christ says, [[Matt 15:24|I was not sent but to the sheep, that are lost of the house of Israel|Non sum missus nisi ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel]], so He sends the Apostles to them only: not that He Himself was in no way sent to the Gentiles, especially since in the Acts of the Apostles the Apostle says: [[Acts 28:28|Be it known therefore to you that this salvation of God is sent to the Gentiles|Notum vobis sit, quia gentibus missum est hoc salutare Dei]]; and Simeon the just: [[Luke 2:30|my eyes have seen thy salvation|Viderunt, inquit, oculi mei Salutare tuum]], [[Luke 2:31|Which thou hast prepared before the face of all peoples|quod parasti ante faciem omnium populorum]]. But since He was sent first and principally to convert the Jews, and then the Gentiles, so now the Apostles are ordered to preach to the Jews alone: because it was fitting that the preaching should be made first to them, as a peculiar people, [[Rom 9:5|Whose are the fathers, and of whom is Christ|quorum patres ex quibus Christus]], to whom the promise of Christ's coming was made; and also so that the Jews might be left without excuse for their unbelief. For if Christ had sent His disciples first to unbelievers, they would have had occasion to find fault and to say that He was not the Christ promised in the law to the people of the Jews. So, since Christ and His disciples preached for a short time before His passion, they preached before the passion only to the Jews. But after the resurrection the Saviour said to them: [[Mark 16:15|Go ye into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature|Euntes in mundum universum, prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ]]. And yet the Apostles did not carry this out until after the preaching had been bestowed plentifully and long upon the Jews; and when these for the most part were hardened, they set out to the Gentiles. For which reason Paul and Barnabas said to the Jews: [[Acts 13:46|To you it behoved us first to speak the word of God|Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei]]; but since you have rejected it, [[Acts 13:46|behold we turn to the Gentiles|ecce convertimur ad gentes]].

paras.t: Euntes autem prædicate, dicentes: Quia appropinquavit regnum cœlorum, id est gloria regni ccelestis, quia per Christi incarnationem ac meritum, ingressus regni cœlorum patescit. Homines nempe elongantur ac distant a regno cœlesti et vera felicitate, per culpam. Quoniam ergo Christus venit tollere peccata mundi, idcirco a tempore sui adventus appropinquavit hoc regnum, et homines ad ejus adeptionem disponi cœperunt. Nemo tamen ante passionem illud ingredi potuit.
