Secundo, auferendo ab eis unionem convictus et cohabitationis, trahendo quosdam ad religionis ingressum: et hæc est separatio localis, pertinens ad supererogationem.
paras.en: [[10:35|For I came to set a man at variance against his father|Veni enim separare hominem adversus patrem suum]], that is, to divide the son from the father, destroying their carnal peace and taking away their disordered union, so that they may not be of one mind in sin, but, one of them being turned away from Me, the other may be turned to Me; and in like manner I came to set [[10:35|the daughter against her mother|filiam adversus matrem suam]], taking away a bad friendship and bringing in a good enmity, that is, true love, so that carnal affection may be rooted out; [[10:35|and the daughter in law|et nurum]], that is, the son's wife, [[10:35|against her mother in law|adversus socrum suam]], that is, the husband's mother. [[10:36|And a man's enemies shall be they of his own household|Et inimici hominis patrisfamilias, erunt domestici ejus]], of the father of the family: because those who live with him will oppose him and disagree with him. This very thing is read in the prophet Micheas: [[Mich 7:2|every one hunteth his brother to death|Vir fratrem suum venatur ad mortem]]; [[Mich 7:5|keep the doors of thy mouth from her that sleepeth in thy bosom|ab ea quæ dormit in sinu tuo custodi claustra oris tui]], [[Mich 7:6|For the son dishonoureth the father, and the daughter riseth up against her mother, the daughter in law against her mother in law: and a man's enemies are they of his own household|quia filius contumeliam facit patri, filia consurget adversus matrem, nurus adversus socrum, et inimici hominis domestici ejus]]. So Christ came to separate men from one another, however near, in two ways. First, by taking from them the union of carnal affection and consent in evil: and this is spiritual separation, necessary for salvation, without which no one can be a servant or disciple of Christ[[Luke 14:26||]]. Secondly, by taking from them the union of living and dwelling together, drawing some to enter religion: and this is separation of place, which belongs to supererogation [that is, to what goes beyond what is commanded].

paras.t: Qui autem amat patrem aut matrem carnalem plus quam me, majus bonum eis optando quam mihi, vel magis afficiendo ad eos quam ad me, seu magis inhærendo eis quam mihi, aut magis appretiando eos quam me, non est me, hoc est mea fruitione aut dilectione, dignus, quum non habeat caritatem ordinatam, et per consequens, nec caritatem, quum ordo caritatis sit in præcepto. Et qui amat filium aut filiam super me, hoc est plus quam me, non est me dignus, quoniam bonum creatum, caducum, finitum, præfert bono divino, incommutabili atque immenso. Ordo nempe caritatis efflagitat, ut Deus summe et incomparabiliter ac sine mensura diligatur, videlicet toto corde, tota virtute etc., deinde propria anima, deinde proximus, deinde proprium corpus. Inter proximos vero maxime diligendi sunt parentes, nec propter alicujus rei creatæ favorem, amorem, sive intuitum, recedendum est ab amore et cultu divino. Denique in Evangelio secundum Lucam Christus affirmat: Qui non odit patrem, et matrem, et uxorem, et filios, non potest meus esse discipulus. Non quod debeamus odio habere illos quoad id quod sunt, sed quoad culpam quam habent, et quantum nobis in via Dei obsistunt.
paras.en: [[10:37|He that loveth father or mother more than me|Qui autem amat patrem aut matrem carnalem plus quam me]], his carnal father or mother, wishing them a greater good than Me, or being more drawn to them than to Me, or clinging more to them than to Me, or prizing them more than Me, [[10:37|is not worthy of me|non est me dignus]], that is, of enjoying or loving Me, since he has not ordered charity, and consequently not charity at all, since the order of charity is commanded. [[10:37|and he that loveth son or daughter more than me, is not worthy of me|et qui amat filium aut filiam super me, non est me dignus]], because he prefers a created, perishable and finite good to the divine, unchangeable and immense good. For the order of charity demands that God be loved supremely and beyond compare and without measure, namely with the whole heart, the whole strength, etc.; then one's own soul, then one's neighbour, then one's own body. And among our neighbours our parents are to be loved most; yet for the favour, love or regard of no created thing must one draw back from the love and worship of God. Lastly, in the Gospel according to Luke Christ affirms: [[Luke 14:26|If any man come to me, and hate not his father and mother and wife and children and brethren and sisters, yea and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple|Qui non odit patrem, et matrem, et uxorem, et filios, non potest meus esse discipulus]]. Not that we must hate them as to what they are, but as to the guilt they have, and in so far as they stand in our way in the way of God.

paras.t: Et qui non accipit crucem suam, hoc est pœnitentiæ afflictionem, vitiorum et concupiscentiarum crucifixionem, et sequitur me ambulando per arctam viam, et ingrediendo per portam angustam, vel etiam mortem corporalem sustinendo pro me, si ratio exigat; non est me dignus: quia non habet gratiam gratum facientem. Idcirco hortatur Apostolus: Semper mortificationem Jesu in corpore nostro circumferentes, ut et vita Jesu manifestetur in carne nostra mortali; rursusque: Si commortui sumus, et convivemus; si sustinebimus, et conregnabimus. Maledicti sunt ergo qui nunc in deliciis, et vanitatibus, vel voluptatibus vivunt, qui ducunt in bonis dies suos, quia in puncto ad inferna descendent. Ex quo certissime constat impossibile esse, nunc gaudere cum sæculo, et post regnare cum Christo, secundum quod Salvator noster asserit: Væ vobis qui ridetis nunc, quia lugebitis; væ vobis qui saturati estis; væ vobis qui habetis consolationem vestram. Totum equidem tempus vitæ præsentis ad gemendum et flendum, ad pcenitentiam peragendam, ad suspirandum ad patriam, ad pugnandum contra vitia, nobis indultum est, districteque requirendum est a nobis per Christum quomodo sit expensum.
paras.en: [[10:38|And he that taketh not up his cross|Et qui non accipit crucem suam]], that is, the affliction of penance, the crucifying of vices and concupiscences, [[10:38|and followeth me|et sequitur me]], walking by the strait way and entering by the narrow gate[[Matt 7:14||]], or even bearing bodily death for Me if reason requires, [[10:38|is not worthy of me|non est me dignus]], because he has not sanctifying grace. Therefore the Apostle exhorts: [[2 Cor 4:10|Always bearing about in our body the mortification of Jesus, that the life also of Jesus may be made manifest|Semper mortificationem Jesu in corpore nostro circumferentes, ut et vita Jesu manifestetur]] in our mortal flesh; and again: [[2 Tim 2:11|if we be dead with him, we shall live also with him|Si commortui sumus, et convivemus]]; [[2 Tim 2:12|If we suffer, we shall also reign with him|si sustinebimus, et conregnabimus]]. Cursed, then, are those who now live in delights and vanities or pleasures, who [[Job 21:13|spend their days in wealth, and in a moment they go down to hell|ducunt in bonis dies suos, quia in puncto ad inferna descendent]]. From which it is most certainly clear that it is impossible now to rejoice with the world and afterwards to reign with Christ, as our Saviour asserts: [[Luke 6:25|Woe to you that now laugh: for you shall mourn|Væ vobis qui ridetis nunc, quia lugebitis]]; [[Luke 6:25|Woe to you that are filled|væ vobis qui saturati estis]]; [[Luke 6:24|woe to you that are rich: for you have your consolation|væ vobis qui habetis consolationem vestram]] [Denis gives only 'woe to you that have your consolation']. Indeed the whole time of the present life has been granted us for groaning and weeping, for doing penance, for sighing for the fatherland, for fighting against vices; and it will be strictly required of us by Christ how it has been spent.

paras.t: Qui invenit, hoc est, vere cognoscit, et spiritualiter diligit, animam suam, perdet eam, id est, in præsenti sæculo eam affliget ac mortificabit, abstrahendo ei delectabilia mundi, exponendoque eam omni propter Christum persecutioni. Et qui perdiderit animam suam hoc modo propter me, hoc est amore mei, et ut mihi finaliter uniatur: quod tamen non est animam perdere secundum veritatem, sed secundum carnalium æstimationem; inveniet eam, id est, in futura beatitudine eam possidebit, et salvam reperiet. Hoc est quod alibi dicit Salvator: Qui odit animam suam in hoc mundo, in vitam æternam custodit eam. Alii sic exponunt: Qui invenit animam suam, id est, præsentem vitam carnaliter inordinateque diligit, perdet eam, hoc est, damnationi faciet eam obnoxiam, seu damnatione condignam, quum præsens vita non sit amanda in se, nec deliciose fovenda, sed ad futuram vitam ordinanda.
paras.en: [[10:39|He that findeth|Qui invenit]], that is, truly knows and spiritually loves, [[10:39|his life|animam suam]], his soul, [[10:39|shall lose it|perdet eam]], that is, in the present world will afflict and mortify it, withdrawing from it the delights of the world and exposing it to every persecution for Christ. [[10:39|and he that shall lose his life for me|Et qui perdiderit animam suam hoc modo propter me]] in this way, that is, for love of Me and so as to be finally united to Me (which is not to lose one's soul in truth, but in the reckoning of the carnal), [[10:39|shall find it|inveniet eam]], that is, will possess it in the happiness to come and find it saved. This is what the Saviour says elsewhere: [[John 12:25|he that hateth his life in this world keepeth it unto life eternal|Qui odit animam suam in hoc mundo, in vitam æternam custodit eam]]. Others explain it thus: He that findeth his life, that is, loves the present life carnally and inordinately, shall lose it, that is, will make it liable to damnation, or deserving of damnation; since the present life is not to be loved for itself, nor cherished delicately, but ordered to the life to come.

paras.t: Qui recipit vos prædicatores et pauperes meos ad suam mensam vel domum, necessaria ministrando, me recipit, hoc est, rem mihi tam gratam ac meritoriam facit, ac si meam personam reciperet. Recipit enim membra mea, seu mysticum corpus meum. Hinc Christus ait ad Paulum: Quid me persequeris? Et ad Samuelem: Non te abjecerunt, sed me. Tantus est amor Dei ad nos, ut dicat per Zachariam prophetam: Qui tetigerit vos, tanget pupillam oculi mei. Et qui me recipit in propria persona, dum adhuc in mundo vivo inter homines, vel in membris meis, vel spiritualiter in corde suo per fidem et caritatem, recipit eum qui me misit, id est Deum Patrem, vel totam Trinitatem, quæ inseparabilis est. A qualibet namque Persona divina missus est Christus secundum quod homo, quemadmodum in Isaia testatur, dicens: Et nunc Dominus misit me, et spiritus ejus. Qui autem Christum corporaliter receperunt in mundo, certum est quod rem Deo Patri gratam fecerunt, eumque per gratiæ infusionem spiritualiter susceperunt. Qui vero receperunt Christum spiritualiter, credendo in ipsum, receperunt et Patrem, totamque superbenedictissimam Trinitatem. Unde Joannes ait in prima sua epistola: Qui negat Filium, nec Patrem habet; et qui non credit in Filium, mendacem facit Patrem, quia non credit in testimonium quo testificatus est Pater de Filio.
paras.en: [[10:40|He that receiveth you|Qui recipit vos]], My preachers and My poor, to his table or house, supplying what is needed, [[10:40|receiveth me|me recipit]], that is, does a thing as pleasing and meritorious to Me as if he received My person. For he receives My members, that is, My mystical body. Hence Christ says to Paul: [[Acts 9:4|why persecutest thou me?|Quid me persequeris?]] And to Samuel: [[1 Kings 8:7|they have not rejected thee, but me|Non te abjecerunt, sed me]]. So great is the love of God for us that He says by the prophet Zacharias: [[Zach 2:8|he that toucheth you, toucheth the apple of my eye|Qui tetigerit vos, tanget pupillam oculi mei]]. [[10:40|and he that receiveth me|Et qui me recipit]] in My own person, while I still live in the world among men, or in My members, or spiritually in his heart by faith and charity, [[10:40|receiveth him that sent me|recipit eum qui me misit]], that is, God the Father, or the whole Trinity, which is inseparable. For Christ as man was sent by each divine Person, as He testifies in Isaias, saying: [[Is 48:16|now the Lord God hath sent me, and his spirit|Et nunc Dominus misit me, et spiritus ejus]]. And it is certain that those who received Christ bodily in the world did a thing pleasing to God the Father, and received Him spiritually through the infusion of grace. And those who received Christ spiritually, by believing in Him, received the Father also, and the whole most super-blessed Trinity. Whence John says in his first epistle: [[1 John 2:23|Whosoever denieth the Son, the same hath not the Father|Qui negat Filium, nec Patrem habet]]; and [[1 John 5:10|He that believeth not the Son maketh him a liar: because he believeth not in the testimony which God hath testified of his Son|qui non credit in Filium, mendacem facit Patrem, quia non credit in testimonium quo testificatus est Pater de Filio]].

paras.t: Qui recipit Prophetam, hoc est nuntium Dei de futuris vaticinantem, in nomine Prophetæ, id est ad hoc, quia Propheta est, et inspiratus ac missus a Deo, mercedem Prophetæ, id est beatitudinem Prophetæ in cœlo paratam, accipiet a Deo, quamvis non tantam sicut Propheta, nisi aliunde sit magni præclarique meriti. Imo, si talis receptus ut Propheta, non esset verus, sed pseudopropheta, si tamen recipitur quia putatur Propheta, recipiens non privatur mercede veri Prophetæ, quoniam Deus mentalis intentionis inspector est. Et qui recipit justum in nomine justi, hoc est ea ratione quoniam justus est et famulus Dei, justificatus a Deo, non quia cognatus, aut compatriota, mercedem Justi accipiet a Deo in patria, pro opere misericordiæ. Talis namque receptio justi, quum ex caritate procedat, et actu: misericordiæ sit, meritoria est vitæ æternæ. Si vero recipiens non esset in caritate, nil de condigno mereretur. Posset tamen Deus ei caritatem infundere occasione receptionis præfatæ.
paras.en: [[10:41|He that receiveth a prophet|Qui recipit Prophetam]], that is, a messenger of God foretelling things to come, [[10:41|in the name of a prophet|in nomine Prophetæ]], that is, for this reason, because he is a prophet, inspired and sent by God, [[10:41|shall receive the reward of a prophet|mercedem Prophetæ, id est beatitudinem Prophetæ in cœlo paratam, accipiet]], that is, the happiness prepared in heaven for a prophet, from God, though not as great as the prophet's, unless on other grounds he be of great and outstanding merit. Indeed, if the one received as a prophet were not a true prophet but a false prophet, yet if he is received because he is thought a prophet, the one who receives him is not deprived of the reward of a true prophet, since God is the searcher of the mind's intention[[1 Kings 16:7||]]. [[10:41|and he that receiveth a just man in the name of a just man|Et qui recipit justum in nomine justi]], that is, for this reason, because he is just and a servant of God, justified by God, not because he is a kinsman or fellow-countryman, [[10:41|shall receive the reward of a just man|mercedem justi accipiet]] from God in the fatherland, for the work of mercy. For such a receiving of a just man, since it proceeds from charity and is an act of mercy, is meritorious of eternal life. But if the one who receives were not in charity, he would merit nothing condignly [that is, by strict desert]. Yet God could pour charity into him on the occasion of that receiving.

paras.t: Et quicumque potum dederit uni ex minimis istis discipulis meis aut famulis, utpote calicem aquæ frigidæ, id est aquam frigidam tam modicam quæ contineri possit in scypho, tantum in nomine discipuli, id est ideo solum quia discipulus Christi est: quod est ad Christi honorem conferre; amen dico vobis, non perdet mercedem suam. Deus enim nullum bonum dimittit irremuneratum, magisque pensat affectum et intentionem, quam munus vel magnitudinem ejus. Nullus ergo adeo pauper est, ut possit se de omissione operum misericordiæ excusare, quum regnum cœlorum porrectione calicis aquæ frigidæ possit mercari, imo solo affectu, si desit aqua.
paras.en: [[10:42|And whosoever shall give to drink to one of these little ones|Et quicumque potum dederit uni ex minimis istis]], My disciples or servants, [[10:42|a cup of cold water|calicem aquæ frigidæ]], that is, cold water as little as can be held in a cup, [[10:42|only in the name of a disciple|tantum in nomine discipuli]], that is, solely because he is a disciple of Christ, which is to give it to the honour of Christ, [[10:42|amen I say to you he shall not lose his reward|amen dico vobis, non perdet mercedem suam]]. For God leaves no good unrewarded, and weighs the affection and intention more than the gift or its size. So no one is so poor that he can excuse himself for leaving out works of mercy, since the kingdom of heaven can be bought by holding out a cup of cold water, nay by the affection alone, if water is lacking.

paras.t: Postremo sapienter pensanda est discretio Christi in suis præceptis, quomodo rigorem justitiæ clementia temperet. Qui enim præcepit pradicatoribus suis sanctis Apostolis, aliisque discipulis, nil possidere vel ferre in via, nunc alios ad receptionem et sustentationem illorum tam copiosissimis promissionibus incitat, ut asserat se recipi ab his qui illos receperint, recipientes quoque associandos receptis in gloria.
paras.en: Lastly, the discretion of Christ in His precepts is to be wisely weighed: how He tempers the rigour of justice with mercy. For He who commanded His preachers, the holy Apostles and the other disciples, to possess or carry nothing on the way, now urges others to receive and support them with such most abundant promises as to assert that He Himself is received by those who receive them, and that those who receive them are to be joined with those received, in glory.

11.title: Explanatio residuæ partis hujus capituli: Ecce ego mitto vos
11.title_en: Explanation of the rest of this chapter: “Behold I send you”

paras.t: Et factum est quum consummasset, id est terminasset, Jesus sermonem præhabitum, præcipiens duodecim discipulis suis, puta Apostolis, nihil possidere aut ferre in via, et cetera quæ nunc exposita sunt, transiit inde, id est a loco in quo istum sermonem fecit, ut doceret et prædicaret in civitatibus eorum, videlicet Judæorum seu Apostolorum, quia in eisdem locis ad quæ præmisit eos, de quibus orti fuerunt, prædicavit Dominus Jesus.
paras.en: [[11:1|And it came to pass, when Jesus had made an end|Et factum est quum consummasset, id est terminasset, Jesus]], that is, had finished the foregoing discourse, [[11:1|of commanding his twelve disciples|præcipiens duodecim discipulis suis]], that is, the Apostles, to possess or carry nothing on the way, and the other things just expounded, [[11:1|he passed from thence|transiit inde]], that is, from the place where He gave this discourse, [[11:1|to teach and to preach in their cities|ut doceret et prædicaret in civitatibus eorum]], namely of the Jews, or of the Apostles, because in the same places to which He had sent them ahead, from which they came, the Lord Jesus preached.

11.title: Elucidatio capituli undecimi: Joannes autem quum audisset opera Christi in vinculis
11.title_en: Explanation of the eleventh chapter: “Now when John had heard in prison the works of Christ”

paras.t: Recitata eruditione ac missione Apostolorum, consequenter agitur de Præcursore. Joannes autem Baptista, quum audisset a suis discipulis: juxta illud, Nuntiaverunt Joanni discipuli ejus de omnibus his, videlicet Christi miraculis, quomodo filium viduæ suscitavit a morte, etc. Unde jam subditur: opera Christi miraculosa, in vinculis positus, hoc est ab Herode Antipa incarceratus ad instantiam Herodiadis, prout Marcus evangelista describit. Mittens duos de discipulis suis ad Christum. Duos misit, ad socialis vitæ commendationem, et ad idoneam testificationem, quia in ore duorum vel trium testium stat omne verbum. ait illi, interrogando per internuntios: Tu es qui venturus es, an alium exspectamus? Joannem non dubitasse de Christi persona, videlicet, quod ipse esset rex Messias, mundi Salvator in lege promissus, et a Prophetis prænuntiatus, omnes sancti catholicique doctores concorditer protestantur. Quomodo enim de hoc ambigere potuit, qui nondum natus Christi præsentiam se cognoscere exsultando monstravit? Qui aliis quoque Christum monstrando, disseruit, Ecce Agnus Dei? Qui Spiritum Sanctum in forma columbæ conspexit super Christum descendere, seque humiliando ei dixit, Ego a te debeo baptizari, et tu venis ad me? Non ergo dubitando interrogavit.
paras.en: Having related the instruction and sending of the Apostles, he next treats of the Forerunner. [[11:2|Now when John had heard|Joannes autem Baptista, quum audisset]], John the Baptist, from his disciples, according to that saying, [[Luke 7:18|And John's disciples told him of all these things|Nuntiaverunt Joanni discipuli ejus de omnibus his]], namely of Christ's miracles, how He raised the widow's son from death, etc. Hence it is now added: [[11:2|the works of Christ|opera Christi]], His miraculous works, [[11:2|in prison|in vinculis]], being in chains, that is, imprisoned by Herod Antipas at the instance of Herodias, as Mark the Evangelist describes[[Mark 6:17||]]. [[11:2|sending two of his disciples|Mittens duos de discipulis suis]] to Christ. He sent two, to commend the common life, and for sufficient testimony, because [[Deut 19:15|in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand|in ore duorum vel trium testium stat omne verbum]]. [[11:2|he said to him|ait illi]], asking through messengers: [[11:3|Art thou he that art to come, or look we for another?|Tu es qui venturus es, an alium exspectamus?]] All the holy and Catholic doctors declare with one voice that John did not doubt about the person of Christ, namely that He was the King Messias, the Saviour of the world promised in the law and foretold by the Prophets. For how could he be uncertain of this, who before he was born showed by leaping that he knew Christ's presence[[Luke 1:41||]]? Who also, pointing Christ out to others, declared: [[John 1:29|Behold the Lamb of God|Ecce Agnus Dei]]? Who saw the Holy Ghost come down upon Christ in the form of a dove[[John 1:32||]], and humbling himself said to Him: [[Matt 3:14|I ought to be baptized by thee, and comest thou to me?|Ego a te debeo baptizari, et tu venis ad me?]] So he did not ask out of doubt.

paras.t: Sed ut brevior fiat tractatus, exponenda sunt diligenter verba Baptistæ. Tu es qui venturus es? Quare non ait, Tu es qui venisti? Et si venturus erat, quomodo venit vel venturus erat? Arbitror ego hæc verba Joannis dupliciter posse intelligi: Primo sic: Tu, de quo talia audio, es qui venturus es, hoc est, prænuntiatus seu prophetatus es esse futurus? hoc est, an tu es Christus quem Prophetæ cecinerunt venturum? An alium exspectamus, id est, alium salvatorem præstolari debemus? Quoniam enim apud Judaeos celeberrima exstitit fama Christum tandem nasciturum, sicut a principio mundi erat prædictum, idcirco per hanc circumlocutionem, Tu es qui venturus es? Christi persona exprimitur: sicut et alio loco scriptum est: Illi homines, quum vidissent quod fecerat signum, dixerunt, Quia hic est vere Propheta qui venturus est in mundum. Hoc etiam patet per id quod in Actibus Apostolorum Paulus affirmat: Joannes baptizavit populum, dicens, In eum qui venturus esset, ut crederent, hoc est in Jesum.
paras.en: But to make the treatment shorter, the Baptist's words must be carefully expounded. [[11:3|Art thou he that art to come|Tu es qui venturus es]]? Why does he not say, Art thou he that hast come? And if He was to come, how had He come, or was He to come? I think these words of John can be understood in two ways. First thus: Art Thou, of whom I hear such things, He that art to come, that is, He who was foretold or prophesied to be coming? That is, art Thou the Christ whom the Prophets sang would come? [[11:3|or look we for another|An alium exspectamus]], that is, ought we to wait for another saviour? For since among the Jews the report was very widespread that the Christ would at last be born, as had been foretold from the beginning of the world, therefore by this roundabout expression, 'Art thou he that art to come?', the person of the Christ is expressed; as it is also written in another place: [[John 6:14|Now those men, when they had seen what a miracle Jesus had done, said: This is of a truth the prophet that is to come into the world|Illi homines, quum vidissent quod fecerat signum, dixerunt, Quia hic est vere Propheta qui venturus est in mundum]]. This is also clear from what Paul affirms in the Acts of the Apostles: John baptized the people, saying: [[Acts 19:4|That they should believe in him, who was to come after him, that is to say, in Jesus|In eum qui venturus esset, ut crederent, hoc est in Jesum]].

paras.t: Si ergo hoc modo exponatur, certissimum est Joannem non interrogasse hæc ex aliqua sui dubitatione. Cur ergo interrogavit? Imo, quomodo interrogavit, quum interrogatio videatur esse dubia propositio? Et respondendum, quod interrogavit, non ob propriam dubitationem, sed propter discipulorum suorum ignorantiam, quos volebat ex Christi responsione doceri et certificari. Noverat enim in spiritu, qualiter Christus fuerat responsurus. Ut enim ait S. Hieronymus, discipuli Joannis superbierunt, et aliquid mordacitatis habuerunt contra Christum. Nam ex livore atque invidia sciscitabantur a Christo: Quare nos et Pharisæi jejunamus frequenter, discipuli autem tui manducant et bibunt? Simili mente dixerunt Joanni Baptistæ: Magister, cui tu testimonium perhibebas, ecce hic baptizat, et omnes veniunt ad eum. Tanquam dicant: Nos relinquimur, et ad illum confluit turba. Præterea, quod nuntiaverunt Joanni opera Christi, non fecerunt simplici corde, sed invidia stimulante, ut dicit Glossa Lucæ. Volens ergo Joannes animas discipulorum suorum sanare, mittit eos ad Christum, ut visis ejus miraculis, credant ac diligant. Quærit autem, non quasi dubitans, sed informationem nuntiorum desiderans. Unde et Christus multoties interrogavit quæ utique non ignoravit: ut quum dixit de Lazaro, Ubi posuistis eum? et ad Philippum, Unde ememus panes ut manducent hi? et alias, Cujus est imago hæc et superscriptio? Quandoque enim interrogat homo, ut instruatur; interdum, ut instruat; interdum, ut experiatur si aliquis sciat quod quærit; interdum, ut alterius ignorantiam monstret. Joannes quaesivit, ut discipuli sui instruerentur. Hæc dicta sunt secundum eos qui exponunt hunc locum modc nunc tacto.
paras.en: If, then, it is expounded in this way, it is most certain that John did not ask this out of any doubt of his own. Why then did he ask? Nay, how did he ask, since a question seems to be a doubtful proposition? And it must be answered that he asked, not because of his own doubt, but because of the ignorance of his disciples, whom he wished to be taught and assured by Christ's answer. For he knew in spirit how Christ would answer. For, as St Jerome says, John's disciples were proud, and had something of a biting spirit against Christ. For out of spite and envy they asked Christ: [[Matt 9:14|Why do we and the Pharisees, fast often|Quare nos et Pharisæi jejunamus frequenter]], but thy disciples eat and drink[[Luke 5:33||]]? In the same spirit they said to John the Baptist: Master, [[John 3:26|to whom thou gavest testimony: behold, he baptizeth and all men come to him|cui tu testimonium perhibebas, ecce hic baptizat, et omnes veniunt ad eum]]. As if to say: We are left, and the crowd flocks to Him. Moreover, when they told John of Christ's works[[Luke 7:18||]], they did not do it with a simple heart, but goaded by envy, as the Gloss on Luke says. So John, wishing to heal the souls of his disciples, sends them to Christ, so that, seeing His miracles, they might believe and love. And he asks, not as one doubting, but wanting information from the messengers. So Christ too often asked about things He certainly knew: as when He said of Lazarus, [[John 11:34|Where have you laid him?|Ubi posuistis eum?]] and to Philip, [[John 6:5|Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat?|Unde ememus panes ut manducent hi?]] and elsewhere, [[Matt 22:20|Whose image and inscription is this?|Cujus est imago hæc et superscriptio?]] For sometimes a man asks so as to be taught; sometimes so as to teach; sometimes to test whether someone knows what he asks; sometimes to show up another's ignorance. John asked so that his disciples might be taught. These things are said according to those who expound this place in the way just touched on.

paras.t: Secundo exponitur sic: Tu, Christe, Fili Dei unigenite, es qui venturus es ad passionem, et limbum inferni? An alium exspectamus, qui pro mundi salute passurus sit, et ad inferos descensurus? Sic exponit Gregorius. Tanquam dicat Joannes: Quæro, an sicut nativitatem tuam præcucurri nascendo, et tuam baptizationem baptizando, sic tuum descensum ad inferos præcurram, nuntiando patribus in inferno te descensurum ad eos. Secundum Gregorium autem, Joannes quæsivit duo: primo, an Christus per se ipsum descenderet in infernum; secundo, an mori dignaretur pro humana salute. Et secundum Gregorium, hæc interrogavit Joannes de eis dubitando.
paras.en: Secondly it is expounded thus: [[11:3|Art thou he that art to come|Tu es, qui venturus es]], O Christ, only-begotten Son of God, to the passion and to the limbo of hell? [[11:3|or look we for another|An alium exspectamus]], who will suffer for the salvation of the world and descend to those below? So Gregory expounds it. As if John said: I ask whether, as I went before Your birth by being born and Your baptism by baptizing, so I am to go before Your descent to those below, announcing to the fathers in hell that You will come down to them. And according to Gregory, John asked two things: first, whether Christ would descend into hell in His own person; second, whether He would deign to die for man's salvation. And according to Gregory, John asked these things doubting about them.

paras.t: Sed hoc communiter non tenetur. Joannes enim fuit plus quam propheta, et repletus Spiritu Sancto in utero matris, præcursor Christi, et judicis præco: ideo magis illuminatus fuit de Christo et ejus mysteriis, quam Prophetæ veteris Testamenti. Quod autem Christus per se pro hominum redemptione moreretur, Prophetæ sciverunt, et apertissime prædixerunt Unde est illud Danielis: Post hebdomades sexaginta duas, occidetur Christus. Et Jeremias inquit: Ego quasi agnus mansuetus qui portatur ad victimam. Isaias quoque ait: Ipse autem vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras, attritus est propter scelera nostra. Imo in Psalmo qui incipit, Deus, Deus meus, respice in me, passio Christi tam clare prædicta est, ut potius videatur illic res gesta narrari, quam prænuntiari futura. Insuper, quod Christus per se ad infernum descenderet, per Zachariam prophetam prædictum est: Tu quoque in sanguine testamenti tui, emisisti vinctos tuos de lacu in quo non est aqua. Ad quod pertinet illud Osee: Ero mors tua, o mors; morsus tuus ero, inferne. Et illud in Psalmo: Ascendisti in altum, cepisti captivitatem.
paras.en: But this is not commonly held. For John was more than a prophet[[11:9||]], and filled with the Holy Ghost in his mother's womb[[Luke 1:15||]], the forerunner of Christ and the herald of the Judge[[Mark 1:2||]]: therefore he was more enlightened about Christ and His mysteries than the Prophets of the Old Testament. And that Christ would die in person for the redemption of men, the Prophets knew and foretold most openly. Hence that saying of Daniel: [[Dan 9:26|after sixty-two weeks Christ shall be slain|Post hebdomades sexaginta duas, occidetur Christus]]. And Jeremias says: [[Jer 11:19|I was as a meek lamb, that is carried to be a victim|Ego quasi agnus mansuetus qui portatur ad victimam]]. Isaias too says: [[Is 53:5|he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our sins|Ipse autem vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras, attritus est propter scelera nostra]]. Indeed in the Psalm that begins, [[Ps 21:2|O God my God, look upon me|Deus, Deus meus, respice in me]], the passion of Christ was foretold so clearly that it seems rather to tell a thing done than to foretell a thing to come. Moreover, that Christ would in person go down into hell was foretold by the prophet Zacharias: [[Zach 9:11|Thou also by the blood of thy testament hast sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit, wherein is no water|Tu quoque in sanguine testamenti tui, emisisti vinctos tuos de lacu in quo non est aqua]]. To which belongs that of Osee: [[Osee 13:14|O death, I will be thy death; O hell, I will be thy bite|Ero mors tua, o mors; morsus tuus ero, inferne]]. And that in the Psalm: [[Ps 67:19|Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive|Ascendisti in altum, cepisti captivitatem]].

paras.t: Verumtamen cognoscendum, quod expositio Gregorii sumpta est ex verbis Hieronymi, vel saltem consonat eis. Sic namque exponit Hieronymus: Tu es qui venturus es, an alium exspectamus? hoc est, manda mihi, quia ad inferna descensurus sum, utrum te et inferis debeam nuntiare, qui nuntiavi superis, an non conveniat Filio Dei ut gustet mortem, et alium ad sacramenta hæc missurus es. Hoc omnino est quod dicit Gregorius. Sed in hoc differunt, quia secundum Hieronymum, Joannes non quasi ignorans interrogat: et hoc melius sonat.
paras.en: Yet it should be known that Gregory's exposition is taken from the words of Jerome, or at least agrees with them. For Jerome expounds thus: '[[11:3|Art thou he that art to come, or look we for another?|Tu es qui venturus es, an alium exspectamus?]] That is, tell me, since I am about to go down to hell, whether I ought to announce You to those below too, as I have announced You to those above; or whether it does not befit the Son of God to taste death, and You will send another for these mysteries.' This is altogether what Gregory says. But they differ in this, that according to Jerome John does not ask as one ignorant: and this sounds better.

paras.t: Et respondens Jesus discipulis Joannis, ait illis: Euntes renuntiate, hoc est, pro nuntio mihi ab eo facto respondete; Joanni quæ audistis et vidistis, id est verba et opera mea, utpote doctrinam meam, et quomodo verbis imperativis miracula facio. De quibus subjungitur: Cæci, hoc est qui paulo ante cæci fuerunt, nunc vident miraculose illuminati a me; claudi, id est qui vim progressivam penitus perdiderunt, ambulant curati a me; leprosi mundantur a lepra; surdi audiunt, mortui resurgunt. Secundum Augustinum, incertum est quot mortuos suscitaverit Christus. Tres quippe legitur suscitasse; sed multa alia fecit Jesus in conspectu discipulorum suorum, quæ non sunt scripta. Quod vero suscitaverit plures quam tres, videtur ex verbis istis apparentiam quamdam habere. Quum enim dixit hæc verba, nondum suscitaverat Lazarum, quamvis fortasse suscitaverit filiam archisynagogi, et filium viduæ. Si ergo Christus tempore hujus responsionis non suscitasset nisi hos duos, non dixisset forsitan tam absolute pluraliter, Mortui resurgunt, præsertim quum secundum Philosophum, morale sit in his quæ ad propriam commendationem pertinent, declinare ad minus, salva semper veritate. Sed et omnes tres Evangelistæ omiserunt describere suscitationem Lazari, quæ tamen solennissima exstitit. Unde probabile est, quod quorumdam aliorum suscitationes referre omiserunt.
paras.en: [[11:4|And Jesus making answer said to them: Go and relate|Et respondens Jesus discipulis Joannis, ait illis: Euntes renuntiate]], to John's disciples, that is, answer for the message he sent Me, [[11:4|to John what you have heard and seen|Joanni quæ audistis et vidistis]], that is, My words and works, namely My teaching, and how I work miracles by words of command. Of which it is added: [[11:5|The blind see|cæci fuerunt, nunc vident]], that is, those who a little before were blind now see, miraculously given light by Me; [[11:5|the lame walk|claudi ambulant]], that is, those who had wholly lost the power of walking walk, cured by Me; [[11:5|the lepers are cleansed|leprosi mundantur]] of leprosy; [[11:5|the deaf hear, the dead rise again|surdi audiunt, mortui resurgunt]][[Luke 7:22||]]. According to Augustine it is uncertain how many dead Christ raised. Three, indeed, He is read to have raised[[Matt 9:25||]][[Luke 7:15||]][[John 11:43||]]; but [[John 20:30|Many other signs also did Jesus in the sight of his disciples, which are not written|multa alia fecit Jesus in conspectu discipulorum suorum, quæ non sunt scripta]][[John 21:25||]]. And that He raised more than three seems to have some likelihood from these words. For when He said these words He had not yet raised Lazarus, though perhaps He had raised the daughter of the archisynagogue and the widow's son. If, then, at the time of this answer Christ had raised only these two, He would perhaps not have said so absolutely in the plural, 'the dead rise again', especially since, according to the Philosopher, it is a matter of good morals, in things that belong to one's own commendation, to lean towards the less, truth always being kept. Besides, all three [other] Evangelists left out the raising of Lazarus, which was nevertheless most solemn. Hence it is probable that they left out the raisings of certain others.

paras.t: Pauperes evangelizantur, hoc est, evangelica lege et gratia instruuntur, vel beati prædicantur, juxta illud: Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum. Unde per Isaiam prophetam ait Christus: Spiritus Domini super me, evangelizare pauperibus misit me. Et istud intelligi potest, tam de pauperibus spiritu, quam de pauperibus opibus qui contemnunt terrenas divitias. Sicque Christus ostendit se non esse acceptorem personarum, dum non præfert divites pauperibus, sed omnibus indifferenter evangelizat.
paras.en: [[11:5|the poor have the gospel preached to them|Pauperes evangelizantur]], that is, are instructed in the Gospel law and grace, or are proclaimed blessed, according to that saying: [[Matt 5:3|Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven|Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum]]. Hence through the prophet Isaias Christ says: [[Is 61:1|The spirit of the Lord is upon me|Spiritus Domini super me]], he hath sent me [[Luke 4:18|to preach the gospel to the poor|evangelizare pauperibus]]. And this can be understood both of the poor in spirit and of the poor in goods who despise earthly riches. And so Christ shows that He is no respecter of persons, since He does not prefer the rich to the poor, but preaches the Gospel to all alike.

paras.t: Prædictorum autem miraculorum multa fecit Jesus in presentia discipulorum Joannis, secundum quod Lucas scribit, dicens: In ipsa hora curavit multos a languoribus, et plagis, et spiritibus malis, et cæcis multis donavit visum.
paras.en: Many of the aforesaid miracles Jesus did in the presence of John's disciples, according to what Luke writes, saying: [[Luke 7:21|in that same hour, he cured many of their diseases and hurts and evil spirits: and to many that were blind he gave sight|In ipsa hora curavit multos a languoribus, et plagis, et spiritibus malis, et cæcis multis donavit visum]].

paras.t: Quomodo vero Salvator ista miracula spiritualiter fecerit, facile est pensare. Spiritualiter etenim cæci vident, dum Christo desuper radiante, homines ab ignorantia, errore, vel infidelitate purgantur. Surdi audiunt, dum rebelles verbo Dei obediunt: spiritualiter namque duritia obstinatæ mentis, surditas appellatur. Leprosi mundantur, dum a vitiis gulæ atque luxuriæ homines expurgantur. Claudi am. bulant, dum pigri et instabiles, ad divina efficiuntur ferventes. Claudicatio enim, obliquitas affectionis, acedia vel nutatio mentis accipitur, juxta illud Regum: Usquequo claudicatis in duas partes? Unde Apostolus admonet, dicens: Rectos facite gressus pedibus vestris, ut non claudicans quis erret, magis autem sanetur. Mortui quoque resurgunt, dum impii pœnitent. Sed et pauperes evangelizantur, dum infirma et abjecta mundi, et ea quæ non sunt, prædicantur a Deo electa, ut fortia et superba confundantur.
paras.en: And how the Saviour does these miracles spiritually is easy to weigh. For spiritually the blind see when, Christ shining from above, men are cleansed of ignorance, error or unbelief. The deaf hear when the rebellious obey the word of God; for spiritually the hardness of an obstinate mind is called deafness. The lepers are cleansed when men are purged of the vices of gluttony and lust. The lame walk when the slothful and unstable are made fervent towards divine things. For lameness is taken for crookedness of affection, sloth, or wavering of mind, according to that saying in Kings: [[3 Kings 18:21|How long do you halt between two sides?|Usquequo claudicatis in duas partes?]] Hence the Apostle admonishes, saying: [[Heb 12:13|make straight steps with your feet: that no one, halting, may go out of the way; but rather be healed|Rectos facite gressus pedibus vestris, ut non claudicans quis erret, magis autem sanetur]]. The dead too rise again when the wicked repent. And the poor have the Gospel preached to them when the weak and despised things of the world, and the things that are not, are proclaimed chosen by God, that the strong and proud may be confounded[[1 Cor 1:27||]].

paras.t: Et beatus est nunc in spe, beatificandus tandem in re, qui non fuerit scandalizatus, hoc est ad ruinam peccati seu infidelitatis inductus, in me, id est ex verbis et factis meis, præsertim ex humilitate eorum quæ in me apparent, ut quod inter homines ambulo, manduco et bibo, et ex acerbitate eorum quæ patior et passurus sum, ut quod more aliorum fatigor, derideor, et morte turpissima occidendus sum. Quemadmodum autem in Christo erat duplex natura, una altissima et divina, alia humilis et humana: sic in Christo fuerunt quædam altissima, utpote prememorata miracula, et alia multa divinitatis insignia; fuerunt quoque in eo quædam humillima et abjecta, ut quod esuriit, lassus fuit, irrisiones sustinuit, et tandem amarissimam pertulit mortem. Quidam ergo pensantes magnalia Christi, concesserunt quod esset verus Filius Dei, sed non hominis: et isti ex magnificentia Christi sunt scandalizati. Alii considerantes abjecta Christi, ut quod mortalis fuit, quod expavit, tristis fuit, et cruci affixus est, concesserunt quod esset filius hominis, sed non Dei: et isti ex humilitate Christi scandalum passi sunt. Sicque nunc loquitur Christus. Tanquam dicat: Beatus est, etc., hoc est, ille qui visis miraculis meis credit me esse Christum Filium Dei, et visis tormentis et tribulationibus meis, non discredit de mea majestate, sed stabilis manet in fide et caritate, beatus est. Talis tempore passionis fuit Maria, non Apostoli, quibus dixit Salvator: Omnes vos scandalum patiemini in me nocte ista. Prædictis verbis tetigit Christus Joannis discipulos, qui scandalizati fuerunt in Christo.
paras.en: [[11:6|And blessed is he|Et beatus est]] now in hope, to be made blessed at last in reality, [[11:6|that shall not be scandalized|qui non fuerit scandalizatus]], that is, led to the ruin of sin or unbelief, [[11:6|in me|in me]], that is, by My words and deeds, especially by the lowliness of the things that appear in Me, as that I walk among men, eat and drink, and by the bitterness of what I suffer and shall suffer, as that I grow weary like others, am mocked, and am to be killed by a most shameful death[[Wis 2:20||]]. For as in Christ there was a twofold nature, one most high and divine, the other lowly and human, so in Christ there were certain most high things, such as the miracles just mentioned and many other marks of the Godhead; and there were also in Him certain most lowly and abject things, as that He hungered, was weary, bore mockery, and at last endured a most bitter death. Some, then, weighing Christ's great works, granted that He was truly the Son of God, but not of man; and these were scandalized by Christ's majesty. Others, considering Christ's abject things, as that He was mortal, that He was afraid, was sad, and was fastened to the cross, granted that He was the son of man, but not of God; and these took scandal from Christ's lowliness. And so Christ now speaks, as if to say: Blessed is he, etc.; that is, he who, seeing My miracles, believes Me to be the Christ, the Son of God, and seeing My torments and tribulations, does not cease to believe in My majesty, but stays firm in faith and charity, is blessed. Such at the time of the passion was Mary, not the Apostles, to whom the Saviour said: [[Matt 26:31|All you shall be scandalized in me this night|Omnes vos scandalum patiemini in me nocte ista]]. By the words above Christ touched John's disciples, who were scandalized in Christ.

paras.t: Ex præinductis constat, quod Christus non respondit directe ad verba interrogationis S. Joannis; sed opera sua jussit ei referri, quatenus ex illis miraculosis effectibus Joannes demonstraret suis discipulis Jesum esse Christum, quoniam talia signa futura esse in Christi adventu Isaias prædixerat, dicens: Tunc aperientur oculi cæcorum, et aures surdorum patebunt: tunc saliet claudus sicut cervus, et aperta erit lingua mutorum.
paras.en: From what has been brought forward it is clear that Christ did not answer St John's question directly; but He ordered His works to be reported to him, so that from those miraculous effects John might show his disciples that Jesus was the Christ, since Isaias had foretold that such signs would be at the coming of Christ, saying: [[Is 35:5|Then shall the eyes of the blind be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped|Tunc aperientur oculi cæcorum, et aures surdorum patebunt]]: [[Is 35:6|Then shall the lame man leap as a hart, and the tongue of the dumb shall be free|tunc saliet claudus sicut cervus, et aperta erit lingua mutorum]].

paras.t: Insuper Christus convertitur ad laudem Joannis. Quoniam enim turbæ noverant Joannem ante suam incarcerationem testimonium perhibuisse Jesu quod esset Christus, et nunc quæsivit, Tu es qui venturus es? poterant suspicari Joannem esse levem, mollem, et mobilem. Ideo hoc excludens Salvator, laudat Joannem, non in presentia discipulorum suorum, ne illis vel Joanni videatur adulari, quoniam certum fuit quod discipuli Joannis referrent ei quidquid a Christo audissent. Subditur itaque:
paras.en: Further, Christ turns to the praise of John. For since the crowds knew that John before his imprisonment had borne witness to Jesus that He was the Christ[[John 1:34||]], and now asked, '[[11:3|Art thou he that art to come?|Tu es qui venturus es?]]', they could suspect that John was light, soft and changeable. So the Saviour, ruling this out, praises John, not in the presence of John's disciples, lest He seem to flatter them or John, since it was certain that John's disciples would report to him whatever they had heard from Christ. So it is added:

paras.t: Illis autem abeuntibus, hoc est, ad Joannem redire incipientibus, cœpit Jesus dicere ad turbas de Joanne: Quid, id est qualem virum, existis in desertum, ubi morabatur Joannes, videre, ante incarcerationem Joannis? Arundinem vento agitatam? id est, an existis ad hoc ut videretis hominem levem atque instabilem, similem arundini seu calamo, quem ventus in omnem partem impellit, et faciliter movet, quasi Joannes ex animi levitate nunc dubitet de me, de quo dixit, Quia non sum dignus ut procumbens solvam corrigiam calceamentorum ejus? Hoc Christus interrogat, et interrogando innuit talem non esse Joannem. Quasi dicat: Joannes vir justus et stabilis est, quem nulla culpa vel passio a rectitudine dejicit. Quemadmodum scriptum est, Homo sanctus in sapientia permanet ut sol, nam stultus sicut luna mutatur. Et Salomon ait: Justus quasi fundamentum aternum. Tales sunt omnes qui nec blandimentis nec minis, nec amore nec odio, nec prosperis nec adversis, a veritate et æquitate flectuntur. Sed homines vani quum laudantur, extolluntur, quum vituperantur, irascuntur, quasi propter aliorum laudem aut vituperationem ipsi meliores essent, vel deteriores.
paras.en: [[11:7|And when they went their way|Illis autem abeuntibus]], that is, began to return to John, [[11:7|Jesus began to say to the multitudes concerning John: What went you out into the desert to see?|cœpit Jesus dicere ad turbas de Joanne: Quid existis in desertum videre?]] That is, what kind of man did you go out to see in the desert, where John stayed, before John's imprisonment? [[11:7|a reed shaken with the wind?|Arundinem vento agitatam?]] That is, did you go out to see a light and unstable man, like a reed or cane, which the wind drives every way and easily moves, as though John, out of lightness of mind, were now in doubt about Me, of whom he said: [[Mark 1:7|the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and loose|non sum dignus ut procumbens solvam corrigiam calceamentorum ejus]]? This Christ asks, and by asking hints that John is not such. As if to say: John is a just and steadfast man, whom no fault or passion casts down from uprightness. As it is written: [[Ecclus 27:12|A holy man continueth in wisdom as the sun: but a fool is changed as the moon|Homo sanctus in sapientia permanet ut sol, nam stultus sicut luna mutatur]]. And Solomon says: [[Prov 10:25|the just is as an everlasting foundation|Justus quasi fundamentum æternum]]. Such are all who are not bent from truth and equity by flatteries or threats, by love or hatred, by prosperity or adversity. But vain men, when they are praised, are puffed up, and when they are blamed, grow angry, as though they themselves were better or worse because of others' praise or blame.

paras.t: Sed quid existis videre (secundum sensum prætactum)? Hominem mollibus, hoc est deliciosis indumentis, vestitum? id est, num talem videre existis? Quod si fecistis, errastis: quoniam Joannes talis non fuit, sicut subjungitur: Ecce qui mollibus vestiuntur, hoc est pretiosis et dulcibus vestimentis, in domibus regum sunt, id est in palatiis principum. Joannes autem non in palatiis, sed in eremo habitavit; non mollia indumenta, sed vestem de pilis camelorum portavit; cibusque ejus fuerunt locustæ, et mel silvestre.
paras.en: [[11:8|But what went you out to see?|Sed quid existis videre]] (in the sense already touched on) [[11:8|a man clothed in soft garments?|hominem mollibus vestitum?]] that is, in luxurious clothing? That is, did you go out to see such a man? If you did, you were wrong: for John was not such, as is added: [[11:8|Behold they that are clothed in soft garments, are in the houses of kings|Ecce qui mollibus vestiuntur, in domibus regum sunt]], that is, in costly and pleasant garments, that is, in the palaces of princes. But John lived not in palaces but in the wilderness; he wore not soft clothing but a garment of camels' hair; and his food was locusts and wild honey[[Matt 3:4||]].

paras.t: Sed quid existis videre? Prophetam? hoc est, numquid egressi estis ad videndum Prophetam? Hoc Christus quærit, sed non negat, quin potius, auget et roborat. Joannes enim propheta fuit, secundum illud Lucæ, dicentis: Tu, puer, Propheta Altissimi vocaberis. Etiam dico vobis, et plus quam Prophetam existis videre: id est, exeundo ad videndum Joannem, egressi estis videre virum qui est plus quam propheta, id est excellens propheta, et majori honore ac gratia, atque cognitione de Christo decoratus, quam ceteri Prophetarum. Nam nondum natus, signo prophetavit, et Spiritu Sancto præventus, usum rationis accepit, et Christum agnovit; Christum quoque baptizavit, ac digito demonstravit; et per Prophetas prophetatus est, atque angelus appellatus; eratque finis legis ac Prophetarum, et novæ legis exordium. Unde dici potest horizon, ligamentum, ac cingulus novi et veteris Testamenti.
paras.en: [[11:9|But what went you out to see? A prophet?|Sed quid existis videre? Prophetam?]] That is, did you go out to see a prophet? This Christ asks, but does not deny; rather He increases and strengthens it. For John was a prophet, according to that saying of Luke: [[Luke 1:76|And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest|Tu, puer, Propheta Altissimi vocaberis]]. [[11:9|Yea I tell you, and more than a prophet|Etiam dico vobis, et plus quam Prophetam]] you went out to see: that is, in going out to see John you went out to see a man who is more than a prophet, that is, an excellent prophet, and adorned with greater honour and grace, and with knowledge of Christ, than the rest of the Prophets. For before he was born he prophesied by a sign, and, prevented by the Holy Ghost, received the use of reason and knew Christ[[Luke 1:41||]]; he also baptized Christ[[Matt 3:13||]] and pointed Him out with his finger[[John 1:29||]]; and he was prophesied by the Prophets[[Mal 3:1||]], and called an angel; and he was the end of the law and the Prophets, and the beginning of the new law. Hence he can be called the horizon, the bond and the girdle of the New and the Old Testament.

paras.t: Hic est enim de quo scriptum est per Malachiam prophetam: Ecce ego Deus Pater vel Trinitas, mitto angelum meum, hoc est nuntium; vel, Angelum meum, id est hominem conversationis angelicæ. Vel Joannes dicitur angelus, quoniam filius sacerdotis, et per consequens sacerdos fuit, saltem secundum auctoritatem vel potestatem. Sacerdos autem angelus appellatur per Malachiam prophetam, dicentem: Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, et legem ex ore ejus requirent, quoniam angelus Domini exercituum est. Quemadmodum enim Dionysius docet, infimum superioris ordinis, et supremum inferioris ordinis, magnam convenientiam habent in natura E et appellatione. In ecclesiastica vero hierarchia sacerdotes sortiuntur primatum, et summi censentur: idcirco nomen eorum qui in cœlesti hierarchia infimum ordinem sortiuntur, convenit eis, ita ut angeli nuncupentur, quia sic appellantur cœlestes spiritus de infimo ordine spirituum supernorum. Quidam hæretici dixerunt Joannem angelum incarnatum, ita quod angelus appelletur, non tantum ratione officii, sed et veritate ac societate naturæ. Itaque, Mitto angelum meum: de quo Joannes inquit, Fuit homo missus a Deo, cui nomen erat Joannes; ante faciem tuam, id est ante tuam apparitionem, vel, ante te, o Christe. Joannes enim orsus est prædicare ante Christum, et manifestationem Christi præcessit: imo ipse Christum manifestavit, quemadmodum apud Joannem inquit: Ut manifestetur in Israel, propterea veni ego in aqua baptizans. Qui præparabit viam tuam, hoc est, fidem, doctrinam, et opera virtuosa, per quæ Christus ingreditur corda hominum, dispositive inducet in animas populi, ante te, id est, antequam tu, o Christe, venias ad prædicandum. Per hoc enim quod Joannes disposuit animas Judæorum ad recipiendum fidem doctrinamque Christi, et ad pœnitentiam peragendam, præparavit Christo ingressum ad corda audientium. Unde scriptum est: Hic venit in testimonium, ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine, ut omnes crederent per ipsum. Hoc plenius expositum est supra capitulo tertio, quo legitur: Vox clamantis in deserto, Parate viam Domini, rectas facite semitas ejus.
paras.en: [[11:10|For this is he of whom it is written|Hic est enim de quo scriptum est]] by the prophet Malachias: [[11:10|Behold I send my angel|Ecce ego mitto angelum meum]], I, God the Father, or the Trinity: that is, My messenger; or, 'My angel', that is, a man of angelic life. Or John is called an angel because he was the son of a priest, and consequently a priest, at least in authority or power. And a priest is called an angel by the prophet Malachias, saying: [[Mal 2:7|For the lips of the priests shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth: because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts|Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, et legem ex ore ejus requirent, quoniam angelus Domini exercituum est]]. For, as Dionysius teaches, the lowest of a higher order and the highest of a lower order have great likeness in nature and in name. In the ecclesiastical hierarchy priests hold the first place and are reckoned highest; therefore the name of those who hold the lowest order in the heavenly hierarchy belongs to them, so that they are called angels, since the heavenly spirits of the lowest order of the spirits above are so called. Certain heretics said that John was an angel incarnate, so that he is called an angel not only by reason of his office but in truth and by sharing the nature. So: 'I send my angel', of whom John says: [[John 1:6|There was a man sent from God, whose name was John|Fuit homo missus a Deo, cui nomen erat Joannes]]; [[11:10|before my face|ante faciem tuam]], that is, before Your appearing, or before You, O Christ. For John began to preach before Christ, and went before Christ's manifestation; nay, he himself made Christ manifest, as he says in John: [[John 1:31|that he may be made manifest in Israel, therefore am I come baptizing with water|Ut manifestetur in Israel, propterea veni ego in aqua baptizans]]. [[11:10|who shall prepare thy way|Qui præparabit viam tuam]], that is, will bring into the souls of the people, by way of disposing them, the faith, teaching and virtuous works by which Christ enters the hearts of men, [[11:10|before thee|ante te]], that is, before You, O Christ, come to preach. For by disposing the souls of the Jews to receive the faith and teaching of Christ and to do penance, John prepared Christ's entry into the hearts of his hearers. Hence it is written: [[John 1:7|This man came for a witness, to give testimony of the light, that all men might believe through him|Hic venit in testimonium, ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine, ut omnes crederent per ipsum]]. This was expounded more fully above, in the third chapter, where we read: [[Matt 3:3|A voice of one crying in the desert, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight his paths|Vox clamantis in deserto, Parate viam Domini, rectas facite semitas ejus]].

paras.t: Porro, Evangelista hoc loco sensum magis quam verba Malachiæ allegat. Sic namque continet nostra translatio: Ecce ego mitto angelum meum, et praparabit viam ante faciem meam. Sed sententia una est, quia sicut Joannes disposuit homines ad notitiam Christi, sic et ad notitiam Patris.
paras.en: Moreover, the Evangelist here cites the sense rather than the words of Malachias. For our translation has it thus: [[Mal 3:1|Behold I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face|Ecce ego mitto angelum meum, et præparabit viam ante faciem meam]]. But the meaning is one, because, as John disposed men to the knowledge of Christ, so too to the knowledge of the Father.

paras.t: Quod autem Joannes merito nuncupetur plus quam propheta, subjungitur. Amen dico vobis, non surrexit, id est, ortus non est, nec ad virtutes ascendit, nec fuit, inter natos mulierum, id est inter eos qui ex feminis a viris imprægnatis geniti sunt, major, id est dignior aut sanctior, Joanne Baptista. Mulier enim hoc loco accipitur pro femina cognita a viro: sicque Christus natus de Virgine, et Virgo mater; quæ fuit inter natas, non inter natos, excipiuntur. Quamvis ergo nullus Prophetarum et Patriarcharum vel Sanctorum naturali ordine genitorum, praferatur Joanni, non tamen Joannes cunctis illis prafertur; sed potest esse æqualis eis. Hoc testimonio de Joanne prolato, Christus ostendit se esse Deum ac judicem hominum: aliter non judicaret nullum prædictorum Joanne majorem, quoniam Salomone teste, spirituum ponderator est Dominus. Propter quod stultum est disputare de comparatione Sanctorum, quis major sit alio, nisi quantum ex Scripturis elicitur.
paras.en: That John is rightly called more than a prophet is then added: [[11:11|Amen I say to you, there hath not risen|Amen dico vobis, non surrexit]], that is, has not arisen, nor climbed to the virtues, nor been, [[11:11|among them that are born of women|inter natos mulierum]], that is, among those born of women made pregnant by men, [[11:11|a greater than John the Baptist|major, id est dignior aut sanctior, Joanne Baptista]], that is, worthier or holier. For 'woman' is here taken for a woman known by a man; and so Christ, born of a Virgin, and the Virgin Mother, who was among those born as a daughter, not as a son, are excepted. So although none of the Prophets and Patriarchs or Saints born in the natural order is preferred to John, yet John is not preferred to all of them, but can be equal to them. By bringing forward this testimony about John, Christ shows that He is God and the judge of men; otherwise He would not judge that none of those mentioned is greater than John, since, as Solomon witnesses, [[Prov 16:2|the Lord is the weigher of spirits|spirituum ponderator est Dominus]]. For which reason it is foolish to dispute about the comparison of the Saints, which is greater than another, except as far as can be drawn from the Scriptures.

paras.t: Qui autem minor est in regno cœlorum, id est infimus Beatorum seu comprehensorum in patria, major, id est perfectior, est illo, puta Joanne Baptista: quoniam clarius videt et ardentius diligit Deum quilibet comprehensor, quam aliquis purus viator. Premium quippe excedit meritum; nec potest perfectio viæ æquari perfectioni patriæ, quia secundum Dionysium, supremum ordinis inferioris non attingit infimum ordinis superioris, quamvis ejus perfectioni multum propinquet. Verumtamen Joannes et multi viatores, in dispositione propinqua majores fuerunt multis Beatis, quoniam tanti meriti exstiterunt, quod amplior eis felicitas debebatur, quam multis Sanctis in patria.
paras.en: [[11:11|yet he that is the lesser in the kingdom of heaven|Qui autem minor est in regno cœlorum]], that is, the lowest of the Blessed or comprehensors [those who already possess God in the fatherland] in the fatherland, [[11:11|is greater than he|major, id est perfectior, est illo]], that is, more perfect, namely than John the Baptist: since every comprehensor sees God more clearly and loves Him more ardently than any mere wayfarer. For the reward exceeds the merit; nor can the perfection of the way be equalled to the perfection of the fatherland, because according to Dionysius the highest of a lower order does not reach the lowest of a higher order, though it comes very near to its perfection. Yet John and many wayfarers were greater than many of the Blessed in proximate disposition, since they were of such merit that a fuller happiness was owed them than to many Saints in the fatherland.

paras.t: Præterea advertendum, quod quum Christus verba hæc protulit, nullus hominum adhuc in regno cœlorum fuit, nisi ipsemet Christus, secundum quod ait: Nemo ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui descendit de cœlo, Filius hominis, qui est in cœlo. Quod igitur dicit Salvator, Qui minor est in regno cœlorum, non de hominibus, sed de angelis rite accipitur, et ita intelligi potest de dignitate naturali: ut sit sensus: Qui minor est in regno cœlorum, id est infimus angelorum, major, id est dignioris naturæ seu speciei, est illo. Planum est enim quod natura angelica altior sit, quantum ad essentialia, natura humana. Sicque his verbis Christus excludit errorem dicentium, quod Joannes sit angelus incarnatus. Unde Veritas, quæ Joannem appellavit angelum, volens hoc intelligi ratione officii, non naturæ, dicit minimum angelorum majorem Joanne. Quocirca vitandus est error Eustachii Græci episcopi, qui in commentariis suis super librum Ethicorum asserit, nullum viatorem posse pertingere ad æqualitatem beatitudinis cujuscumque angelici spiritus: ita quod post Christum et Virginem benedictam, nemo quantumcumque perfectus perveniat ad aliquem ordinem angelorum, sed ex universitate hominum electorum, unus ac infimus ordo constituatur in cœlo.
paras.en: Moreover, it should be noticed that when Christ spoke these words no man was yet in the kingdom of heaven except Christ Himself, according to what He says: [[John 3:13|no man hath ascended into heaven, but he that descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven|Nemo ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui descendit de cœlo, Filius hominis, qui est in cœlo]]. So what the Saviour says, '[[11:11|he that is the lesser in the kingdom of heaven|Qui minor est in regno cœlorum]]', is rightly taken not of men but of angels, and can be understood of natural dignity, so that the sense is: He that is the lesser in the kingdom of heaven, that is, the lowest of the angels, is greater, that is, of a worthier nature or species, than he. For it is plain that the angelic nature is higher than human nature as to essentials. And so by these words Christ shuts out the error of those who say that John is an angel incarnate. Hence the Truth, who called John an angel, meaning this to be understood by reason of his office, not of his nature, says that the least of the angels is greater than John. Accordingly the error of Eustace, a Greek bishop, is to be avoided, who in his commentaries on the book of the Ethics asserts that no wayfarer can reach equality with the happiness of any angelic spirit whatever, so that after Christ and the blessed Virgin no one, however perfect, comes to any order of the angels, but from the whole number of elect men one single lowest order is formed in heaven.

paras.t: Quidam exponunt prædicta hoc modo: Qui minor est in regno cœlorum, id est Christus, qui in Ecclesia militanti minor fuit Joanne, hominum reputatione, et nativitate posterior, atque humilitate profundior, major est illo: quemadmodum idem fatetur Baptista, Qui, inquiens, de cœlo venit, super omnes est; et rursus, Illum oportet crescere, me autem minui.
paras.en: Some expound the foregoing in this way: '[[11:11|he that is the lesser in the kingdom of heaven|Qui minor est in regno cœlorum]]', that is, Christ, who in the Church militant was less than John in men's esteem, later in birth and deeper in humility, '[[11:11|is greater than he|major est illo]]'; as the Baptist himself confesses: [[John 3:31|He that cometh from heaven is above all|Qui, inquiens, de cœlo venit, super omnes est]]; and again: [[John 3:30|He must increase: but I must decrease|Illum oportet crescere, me autem minui]].

11.title: Prosecutio expositionis præsentis capituli, ab eo loco quo habetur: A diebus autem Joannis Baptistæ
11.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this chapter, from the place where we read: “And from the days of John the Baptist”

paras.t: Diebus autem Joannis Baptistæ usque nunc, regnum cœlorum vim patitur. Quid est hoc? Quis enim vim infert regno cœlorum? Et si illud vim patitur, cur potius a diebus Joannis, quam ante? Vel quomodo a diebus Joannis usque nunc, id est hora qua Christus hæc dixit, quasi nec ante nec postea passum sit vim? Est igitur sensus: A diebus autem, id est ab exordio prædicationis, Joannis Baptistæ, regnum cœlorum, id est vita æterna seu gloria patriæ, vim patitur, id est, per violentiam quamdam acquiri prædicatur. Joannes enim primo sic legitur prædicasse: Pœnitentiam agite, quia appropinquabit regnum cœlorum. Sed pœnitentiam agere, est sibi ipsi bonam violentiam facere, affligendo et reprimendo se ipsum. Non ergo sic intelligendum est, quasi ante Joannis prædicationem potuerit aliquis regnum cœlorum mereri sine vi tali seu pœnitentia, sed quia ante non docebatur aperte, quod regnum ecœlorum taliter acquireretur. Per hoc quoque quod dicitur, Usque nunc, non datur intelligi, quod post verba hæc Christi non patiatur vim. Subditur enim: et violenti, id est superantes se ipsos, qui contra se ipsos et concupiscentias cunctaque vitia efficaciter pugnant, rapiunt, id est, cum labore et bona violentia capiunt, illud, pro præmio sui certaminis. Violenti sunt ergo, qui desiderio patriæ, se ipsos quotidie mortificant, carnem suam cum vitiis et concupiscentiis crucifigentes: qui dicere possunt cum Propheta, Propter verba labiorum tuorum ego custodivi vias duras; et cum Apostolo: Nullam requiem habuit caro nostra, sed omnem tribulationem passi sumus; foris pugnæ, intus timores.
paras.en: [[11:12|And from the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence|A diebus autem Joannis Baptistæ usque nunc, regnum cœlorum vim patitur]]. What is this? For who does violence to the kingdom of heaven? And if it suffers violence, why from the days of John rather than before? Or how from the days of John until now, that is, the hour in which Christ said this, as though it suffered violence neither before nor after? The sense, then, is this: 'from the days', that is, from the beginning of the preaching, 'of John the Baptist, the kingdom of heaven', that is, eternal life, the glory of the fatherland, 'suffereth violence', that is, is preached as to be gained by a certain violence. For John is read to have preached first thus: [[Matt 3:2|Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand|Pœnitentiam agite, quia appropinquabit regnum cœlorum]]. But to do penance is to do oneself a good violence, by afflicting and checking oneself. So it is not to be understood as though before John's preaching anyone could merit the kingdom of heaven without such violence, that is, penance, but because before it was not openly taught that the kingdom of heaven is gained in this way. Nor by 'until now' is it given to be understood that after these words of Christ it does not suffer violence. For it is added: [[11:12|and the violent|et violenti]], that is, those who overcome themselves, who fight effectively against themselves and their concupiscences and all vices, [[11:12|bear it away|rapiunt illud]], that is, take it with labour and good violence, as the prize of their struggle. The violent, then, are those who for desire of the fatherland mortify themselves daily, [[Gal 5:24|crucified their flesh, with the vices and concupiscences|carnem suam cum vitiis et concupiscentiis crucifigentes]]: who can say with the Prophet: [[Ps 16:4|for the sake of the words of thy lips, I have kept hard ways|Propter verba labiorum tuorum ego custodivi vias duras]]; and with the Apostle: [[2 Cor 7:5|our flesh had no rest: but we suffered all tribulation. Combats without: fears within|Nullam requiem habuit caro nostra, sed omnem tribulationem passi sumus; foris pugnæ, intus timores]].

paras.t: Dicitur itaque regnum cœlorum vim pati, quoniam propter ipsum adipiscendum, infert homo sibi ipsi vim bonam, et patitur affligendo se ipsum: et ita est prædicatio causalis, quum dicitur, Regnum cœlorum vim patitur. Unde Lucas sic habet: Omnis in illud vim facit. Vel dicitur vim pati, quia per modum patientis se habet, dum homo cum grandi labore illud apprehendit. Secundum quem sensum Dominus ait: Laboravi sustinens; et alio in loco, Si affiget homo Deum, quia vos configitis me, et invaluerunt super me verba vestra?
paras.en: So the kingdom of heaven is said to suffer violence because, to gain it, a man does himself a good violence and suffers by afflicting himself; and so it is a causal predication when it is said, 'The kingdom of heaven suffereth violence'. Hence Luke has it thus: [[Luke 16:16|every one useth violence towards it|Omnis in illud vim facit]]. Or it is said to suffer violence because it behaves as one that undergoes, while a man lays hold of it with great labour. In which sense the Lord says: [[Is 1:14|I am weary of bearing them|Laboravi sustinens]]; and in another place: [[Mal 3:8|Shall a man afflict God, for you afflict me|Si affiget homo Deum, quia vos configitis me]], and your words have prevailed against me[[Mal 3:13||]]?

paras.t: Insuper Christus aperit causam, cur dixit a diebus Joannis regnum ccœlorum vim pati. Omnes enim Prophetæ, et lex Moysis, usque ad Joannem prophetaverunt, id est, obscure et figurative de Christo et regno cœlesti annuntiaverunt, sub promissionibus terrenorum bonorum intelligendo cœlestia, atque per corporalia bona designando spiritualia beneficia Christi. Joannes vero de his apertissime nuntiavit, digito Christum demonstrans, regnumque cœleste proprio nomine exprimens ac promittens. Et quod iste sit sensus, patet per illud quod in Luca scriptum est: Lex et Prophetæ usque ad Joannem; ex eo regnum Dei evangelizatur. S. Hieronymus ita exponit: Omnes Prophetæ et lex usque ad Joannem prophetaverunt, hoc est, de Christo vaticinati sunt, quem Joannes demonstravit, et ejus tempore fuit. Loquitur ergo de Prophetis veteris Testamenti, et per legem, significat Scripturam librorum Moysis.
paras.en: Further, Christ opens the reason why He said that from the days of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence. [[11:13|For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John|Omnes enim Prophetæ, et lex Moysis, usque ad Joannem prophetaverunt]], that is, announced Christ and the heavenly kingdom obscurely and in figures, meaning heavenly things under promises of earthly goods, and signifying the spiritual benefits of Christ by bodily goods. But John announced these things most openly, pointing out Christ with his finger[[John 1:29||]], and naming and promising the heavenly kingdom by its own name[[Matt 3:2||]]. And that this is the sense is clear from what is written in Luke: [[Luke 16:16|The law and the prophets were until John. From that time the kingdom of God is preached|Lex et Prophetæ usque ad Joannem; ex eo regnum Dei evangelizatur]]. St Jerome expounds thus: All the Prophets and the law prophesied until John, that is, foretold Christ, whom John pointed out, and who was in his time. So He speaks of the Prophets of the Old Testament, and by 'the law' He means the Scripture of the books of Moses.

paras.t: Et si vultis recipere, id est cognoscere, Joannes ipse est Elias, non per essentiam sed per magnam assimilationem: secundum quem modum quidam dixerunt Christum esse Jeremiam, alii Eliam, et Christus vocavit Judam diabolum; qui Elias venturus est in fine sæculi ad convertendos Judæos, ut præcedat secundum Christi adventum, sicut Joannes primum, juxta illud Malachiæ prophetæ: Ecce ego mittam vobis Eliam Thesbiten, antequam veniat dies Domini magnus et horribilis. Dicitur ergo Joannes Elias, quia uterque eremita, uterque similibus vestibus utens, uterque præcursor præcoque Judicis, uterque ardentissimus zelator justitiæ, rigorosus, strenuus et imperterritus. Nam sicut Elias corripuit Achab et Jezabel, sic Joannes Herodem ac Herodiadem. Unde de Joanne prædixerat angelus: Ipse præcedet ante illum in spiritu et virtute Elis.
paras.en: [[11:14|And if you will receive it|Et si vultis recipere]], that is, recognize it, John [[11:14|he is Elias|ipse est Elias]], not in essence but by great likeness; in the way in which some said that Christ was Jeremias, others Elias[[Matt 16:14||]], and Christ called Judas a devil[[John 6:71||]]; [[11:14|that is to come|qui venturus est]], Elias, at the end of the world to convert the Jews, so that he may go before the second coming of Christ, as John went before the first; according to that saying of the prophet Malachias: [[Mal 4:5|Behold, I will send you Elias the prophet, before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the Lord|Ecce ego mittam vobis Eliam Thesbiten, antequam veniat dies Domini magnus et horribilis]] [Denis reads 'Eliam Thesbiten', Elias the Thesbite]. So John is called Elias because each was a hermit, each wore like garments, each was a forerunner and herald of the Judge, each a most ardent zealot for justice, severe, vigorous and undaunted. For as Elias rebuked Achab and Jezabel[[3 Kings 18:18||]][[3 Kings 21:20||]], so John rebuked Herod and Herodias[[Matt 14:4||]]. Hence the angel had foretold of John: [[Luke 1:17|he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elias|Ipse præcedet ante illum in spiritu et virtute Eliæ]].

paras.t: Sed quia hæc verba, quibus dictum est Joannem esse Eliam, prudentem intellectum requirunt, ideo Christus adjecit: Qui habet aures audiendi, hoc est aures cordis, videlicet intellectum advertentem ac studiosum. De quibus auribus scriptum est in Deuteronomio: Dixit Moyses ad filios Israel: Non dedit vobis Dominus aures quæ possent audire, usque in præsentem diem. Audiat, id est, sapienter advertat quod dixi, Joannem esse Eliam, ne incidat in errorem hæreticorum, et quorumdam Judæorum Platonem sequentium, atque dicentium animas transcorporari, ut qui nunc est in isto corpore, sit idem qui olim fuit in alio corpore. Fideli igitur aure omnia verba Dei advertenda sunt, juxta illud Sapientis: Auris bona audiet cum omni concupiscentia sapientiam.
paras.en: But since these words, in which John is said to be Elias, require a prudent understanding, Christ added: [[11:15|He that hath ears to hear|Qui habet aures audiendi]], that is, the ears of the heart, namely an attentive and diligent understanding. Of which ears it is written in Deuteronomy: Moses said to the children of Israel: [[Deut 29:4|the Lord hath not given you a heart to understand, and eyes to see, and ears that may hear, unto this present day|Non dedit vobis Dominus aures quæ possent audire, usque in præsentem diem]]. [[11:15|let him hear|Audiat]], that is, let him wisely mark what I said, that John is Elias, lest he fall into the error of the heretics, and of certain Jews following Plato, who say that souls pass from body to body, so that he who is now in this body is the same who once was in another body. So all the words of God are to be heard with a faithful ear, according to that saying of the Wise Man: [[Ecclus 3:31|a good ear will hear wisdom with all desire|Auris bona audiet cum omni concupiscentia sapientiam]].

paras.t: Cui autem similem æstimabo, hoc est, judicabo et pronuntiabo, generationem istam, id est rebelles atque perversos Judæos? Non de omnibus tunc præsentibus dicit hoc Christus, sed de Scribis et Pharisæis, de quibus sequenti capitulo scribitur: Generatio mala et adultera signum quærit. Unde apud Lucam legitur: Omnis populus audiens (scilicet prædictas laudes Joannis) et publicani, justificaverunt Deum, baptizati baptismo Joannis; Pharisæi autem et legisperiti consilium Dei spreverunt, non baptizati ab eo. De his itaque Christus nunc loquitur. Quærit quoque, ut audientes ad diligentem advertentiam excitet. Et respondet: Similis est pueris sedentibus in foro, qui clamantes hoc est cantantes, coæqualibus, id est aliis pueris sibi numero paribus, dicunt cum exprobratione: Cecinimus vobis, id est carmen lætitiæ cantavimus, et non saltastis, id est, nobis congratulati non estis. lamentavimus, hoc est, carmen lugubre vobis cecinimus, et non planxistis, id est ad compassionem moti non estis. Pueris ergo qui nec gaudentibus congaudent, nec dolentibus condolent, isti assimilantur. Cujus ratio subditur.
paras.en: [[11:16|But whereunto shall I esteem this generation to be like?|Cui autem similem æstimabo generationem istam?]] that is, judge and declare, this generation, that is, the rebellious and perverse Jews? Christ does not say this of all who were then present, but of the scribes and Pharisees, of whom it is written in the next chapter: [[Matt 12:39|An evil and adulterous generation seeketh a sign|Generatio mala et adultera signum quærit]]. Hence we read in Luke: [[Luke 7:29|And all the people hearing, and the publicans, justified God, being baptized with John's baptism|Omnis populus audiens (scilicet prædictas laudes Joannis) et publicani, justificaverunt Deum, baptizati baptismo Joannis]] (hearing, that is, the praises of John just spoken); [[Luke 7:30|But the Pharisees and the lawyers despised the counsel of God|Pharisæi autem et legisperiti consilium Dei spreverunt]] … [[Luke 7:30|being not baptized by him|non baptizati ab eo]]. Of these, then, Christ now speaks. He asks also so as to stir His hearers to careful attention.
